⏱ 28 min read A programming language is only the vehicle we use to give instructions to a computer. What really decides whether a program is good is the method it follows to solve the problem. Algorithmics is the discipline that studies those methods: how to design them, how to be sure that they are correct, and how to predict how much time and memory they need. As software engineers, it is not enough that a program "works" on the examples we tried. We must be able to argue that it gives the right answer for every valid input, and that it will still run in a reasonable time and memory when the data grows from a hundred elements to a hundred million. What you will learn in this lesson Where the word algorithm comes from, and how the idea evolved from medieval arithmetic to modern computing. How to move from an intuitive definition ("a recipe") to a formal one, based on Knuth's five properties and on the notion of a problem specification . Why a piece of code that works on a few examples is not necessarily an algorithm, illustrated with several versions of the factorial. What makes some problems "simple" and others hard, and what we mean by the cost and efficiency of a solution. How decomposition and abstraction help us tackle complex problems, and why algorithm design has no universal recipe. Where algorithms show up in real life and in technical job interviews, and how this course prepares you for both.

We often think of algorithms as something new, but the word is more than a thousand years old. It comes from the name of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi , a Persian scholar born around 780 AD in the region of Khwarazm (in present-day Uzbekistan). He worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, the great intellectual center of the 9th century, and made contributions to mathematics, astronomy and geography. One of his books explained how to calculate with the Hindu decimal numeral system, including the use of zero and positional notation. When it was translated into Latin centuries later, its opening words, "Dixit Algoritmi" ("so said al-Khwarizmi"), turned his name into a label for the method itself. In medieval Latin, algorismus simply meant calculating with decimal numerals , as opposed to using an abacus or Roman numerals. Another of his books, on solving equations, gave us the word algebra (from al-jabr , "restoration"). The meaning of the word kept evolving: Medieval period: algorism means the art of written arithmetic with Hindu-Arabic numerals: precise, step-by-step procedures to add, subtract, multiply and divide that anyone could follow mechanically. Late 19th century: algorithm comes to mean, more generally, any finite set of precise rules for solving a problem. 1930s: mathematicians such as Alan Turing and Alonzo Church formalised what it means for a procedure to be "mechanical". Turing's abstract machine showed that a device following simple instructions could, in principle, carry out any computation that can be described algorithmically. This laid the theoretical foundations of the computer age. Today: algorithms decide the route of our trips, the results of our searches, the products we are recommended and the news we read. One of the oldest algorithms still in use Long before the word existed, Euclid described (around 300 BC) a procedure to compute the greatest common divisor of two integers. It is still taught, and still used, today: public static int gcd ( int a , int b ) { // precondition: a >= 0, b >= 0, not both 0 while ( b != 0 ) { int r = a % b ; // remainder of the division a = b ; b = r ; } return a ; } It already has all the ingredients we will study: a precise input domain, unambiguous steps, a guaranteed end (the remainder strictly decreases and cannot go below zero) and a result whose correctness can be proven mathematically.

Almost every programming course starts by printing Hello, world! . If you write it in C, Java, Python, Lisp or Ruby, the syntax changes considerably, but the idea is exactly the same : produce a fixed message as output. This simple observation already contains a key lesson of this course: an algorithm is independent of the language used to express it . The language is the vehicle; the algorithm is the idea. When we study an algorithm, we care about its logic, its correctness and its cost, and these properties remain valid whether we implement it in Java, C++ or a language that does not exist yet. 🧠 Checkpoint: Is "Hello, world!" an algorithm? Answer: Technically yes, although a trivial one. It receives zero inputs (which is allowed), executes a finite number of unambiguous and effective steps, and produces a well-defined output. It satisfies all of Knuth's properties described below. It is simply not interesting from an algorithmic point of view, because there is no problem to solve and no decision to make.

A common analogy compares an algorithm to a cooking recipe. While this image is useful as an entry point, it is not rigorous enough for computer science. A recipe tolerates intuition, approximation and subjective interpretation ("add salt to taste", "bake until golden"). An algorithm, by contrast, must define a computational process with enough precision to be executed mechanically and analyzed mathematically.

Let us compare some definitions: Dictionary definition. The dictionary of the Royal Spanish Academy (RAE) defines an algorithm as an ordered and finite set of operations that allows us to find the solution of a problem . Most widely accepted definition in computing. A finite sequence of steps or instructions to reach the solution of a given problem in a finite time, for any set of input values . The second definition adds two crucial requirements: finite time (not only a finite description) and for any set of input values (not only for the examples we tried). Still, it leaves several engineering questions open: what counts as a valid input, what makes a step unambiguous, and how the procedure behaves on a real machine with limited memory. To reason rigorously about programs, computer science moves from a descriptive view of algorithms to a formal specification view . Under this perspective, an algorithm is a computational object defined over an input domain, associated with an expected relation between inputs and outputs, and constrained by precise execution rules. Perspective Definition Operational goal General / informal An ordered and finite set of steps used to solve a problem. Sequential resolution of a task. Computer science / formal A finite, unambiguous, effective and executable sequence of instructions that transforms valid inputs into outputs according to a precise specification. Predictability, correctness, safety and analysability. In engineering, the difficulty is rarely in describing an idea for solving a problem. The real challenge is defining that idea with enough rigour that its behavior can be trusted, implemented, tested and later analyzed in terms of correctness and efficiency.

Before talking about algorithms, we must be precise about the problem they solve. A computational problem describes, in general terms, the relation between the inputs and the desired outputs. For example: "given a sequence of integers, return the same integers in non-decreasing order" . An instance of the problem is one concrete input, such as [7, 3, 6] . A problem has (usually infinitely) many instances. A specification states the problem precisely, typically through: a precondition : the conditions that a valid input must satisfy (the input domain), and a postcondition : the conditions that the output must satisfy with respect to the input. For the factorial, a possible specification is: \textbf{Pre: } n \in \mathbb{Z},\; 0 \le n \le 20 \qquad\qquad \textbf{Post: } \mathit{result} = n! = \prod_{i=1}^{n} i (we will see later why the upper limit of 20 appears). With a specification in hand, we can finally define correctness: Correctness An algorithm is correct with respect to a specification if, for every instance that satisfies the precondition, it terminates and its output satisfies the postcondition. Note the word every . Testing a program with a hundred inputs can reveal errors, but it cannot prove their absence. Correctness is a property over the whole input domain, which is why we need reasoning and not only experiments.

A classical characterization, popularised by Donald Knuth in his foundational work The Art of Computer Programming , states that a proper algorithm must satisfy five fundamental properties. 1. Finiteness The execution must terminate after a finite number of steps for every valid input in its domain. An algorithm that can enter an endless loop for some admissible input is not complete from a formal standpoint, even if it appears to work for many test cases. This property requires an argument that the execution always progresses towards termination, as in Euclid's algorithm above. In later topics, this idea will connect with loop invariants, well-founded recursion and termination proofs. 2. Definiteness Every step must be specified clearly and without ambiguity. At any point during execution, the next action must be fully determined by the current state and the instruction sequence. Instructions such as "repeat several times" , "sort efficiently" or "stop when the result looks reasonable" are not algorithmic statements; they are vague intentions. A formal algorithm replaces them with exact control conditions, explicit comparisons and precisely defined state transitions. 3. Input An algorithm accepts zero or more inputs taken from a defined domain. This domain is not a secondary detail: it is part of the specification itself. If a factorial procedure is intended only for non-negative integers, this restriction must be stated explicitly. Without a clearly defined input domain, it is impossible to decide whether a behavior is correct, incorrect or simply outside the intended scope of the problem. 4. Output An algorithm must produce one or more outputs that are related in a well-defined way to the input. The existence of output is not enough; the output must satisfy the specification. Printing arbitrary values, returning undocumented "magic" values or terminating without a result does not constitute a valid solution unless such behavior is part of the formal contract. Mathematically, we want to reason about the algorithm as a mapping from admissible inputs to valid outputs. 5. Effectiveness Each step must be elementary enough to be carried out exactly, in finite time, by a mechanical executor. Traditionally, every instruction should be basic enough that a person could perform it with paper and pencil, given enough time. The point of this property is not human practicality, but computational realism. A valid algorithm cannot contain magical steps such as "guess the optimal solution" or "inspect all future states at once" . Every operation must be reducible to basic executable actions.

s.h: Why these properties matter in engineering
s.x: These five properties are not merely historical definitions. Together, they form the minimal contract that makes algorithmic reasoning possible: Without finiteness , we cannot guarantee that execution ever completes. Without definiteness , two programmers could implement the "same" algorithm and obtain different behaviors. Without a clear input domain, correctness becomes impossible to define. Without a specified output , success cannot be measured. Without effectiveness , the procedure may be a mathematical fantasy rather than a realisable computation. Determinism and reproducibility In introductory contexts, algorithms are presented as deterministic procedures: given the same input and initial state, execution follows the same path and produces the same result. This is one of the reasons why algorithms can be tested, verified and compared scientifically. Some algorithms deliberately use randomness (for example, randomised Quicksort, which you will see in the sorting chapter). Even then, the algorithm requires a formally defined state model, execution rules and a precise interpretation of its outputs, often stated in terms of probabilities or expected values.

A crucial distinction for this course is that not every piece of code is automatically an algorithm , and that an algorithm is not the same thing as a program: An algorithm is an abstract method. It can be described in natural language, with a diagram or in pseudocode (a semi-formal notation that ignores the details of any particular language). A program is the expression of one or more algorithms in a concrete programming language, together with everything a real system needs: input/output, error handling, data representation, libraries, etc. A code fragment may fail to terminate on some inputs, omit edge cases, rely on undocumented assumptions or produce outputs that are not meaningfully tied to the problem. In such cases we do not yet have a robust algorithm, only an implementation attempt. Many software failures do not come from syntax errors but from incomplete formalisation : a program can compile, run and even pass several tests while still violating one of the properties above. In that sense, algorithm design begins before coding, when we define the problem precisely enough to make correctness and analysis possible. 🧠 Checkpoint: Formal reasoning Question: Why is the statement "compute the factorial of an integer" not yet a complete specification? Answer: Because it does not define the admissible input domain, the behavior for invalid values such as negative integers, the range of values that the result type can represent, or the expected output in exceptional cases. It describes a goal, but not yet a fully formalised computational process.

s.h: Case Study: Is This an Algorithm? The Factorial
s.x: An implementation that works under ideal conditions but crashes when confronted with boundary inputs is not a robust algorithm; it is a partial program that only works inside a narrow comfort zone. To make this concrete, consider the classical definition of the factorial of a non-negative integer n : n! = \prod_{i=1}^{n} i = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdots n, \qquad 0! = 1 or, equivalently, the recursive definition n! = n \cdot (n-1)! with base case 0! = 1 . The definition already encodes two facts: the domain is the set of non-negative integers, and there is a base case that stops the recursion. When we translate this mathematical object into code, the goal is not to obtain some implementation that returns correct values for a few test cases. The goal is an algorithm whose behavior is well-defined for every input in the chosen domain and that respects the constraints of the machine. Let us analyze four versions. ❌ Version 1: naive ⚠️ Version 2: error value ✅ Version 3: explicit contract 🏁 Version 4: iterative and range-safe public static long factorial ( int n ) { if ( n == 0 ) return 1 ; return n * factorial ( n - 1 ) ; }

At first glance this implementation looks correct: it encodes n! = n \cdot (n-1)! with the base case 0! = 1 , and it terminates for every non-negative n . Now call it with n = -1 : The condition n == 0 is false . The recursive call factorial(-2) is executed, then factorial(-3) , factorial(-4) , and so on, never reaching the base case. Mathematically, the code has silently extended the domain of the function to all integers without saying what the factorial of a negative number should be. Computationally, it has created a recursion with no terminating state for part of its input domain. Internally, each recursive call allocates a new activation record (stack frame) on the call stack, storing parameters, local variables and the return address. Since the recursion depth grows without bound when n is negative, the stack eventually exhausts the memory assigned to the thread and the runtime raises a StackOverflowError , abruptly terminating the program. Violation of finiteness There are valid values of the Java type int for which the execution does not terminate in a finite number of steps. What appears to be an algorithm is only a partial procedure. public static long factorial ( int n ) { if ( n < 0 ) return - 1 ; // "impossible" value used to signal an error else if ( n == 0 ) return 1 ; return n * factorial ( n - 1 ) ; }

s.h: An improvement, with a hidden cost
s.x: This version terminates for every integer : negative inputs are detected immediately. It satisfies finiteness and definiteness, and the behavior for invalid inputs is now part of the contract: "returns -1 if n is negative" . This technique, returning a value that can never be a valid result, is common (for example, indexOf returns -1 when an element is not found). However, it has drawbacks worth discussing: The error travels through the same channel as valid results. If the caller forgets to check it, -1 will silently propagate through later calculations (for example, factorial(n) / 2 returns 0 ). It only works when there is a value that can never be a valid output. For many problems, no such value exists. It is a reasonable choice when the convention is clearly documented and widely known, as in the course repository. public static long factorial ( int n ) { if ( n < 0 ) throw new IllegalArgumentException ( "n must be non-negative" ) ; if ( n == 0 ) return 1 ; return n * factorial ( n - 1 ) ; }

Domain enforcement: the check n < 0 rejects invalid inputs immediately with a documented exception. The error cannot be ignored by accident. Guaranteed progress: for every n >= 0 , the argument decreases by one in each call until it reaches the base case, so execution terminates. Controlled failure: instead of crashing with a StackOverflowError after thousands of nested calls, the algorithm fails fast with a meaningful error that the caller can handle. This is structural robustness : the algorithm does not rely on "good behavior" from its clients; it enforces its contract proactively. public static long factorial ( int n ) { if ( n < 0 || n > 20 ) throw new IllegalArgumentException ( "n must be in [0, 20] to fit in a long" ) ; long result = 1 ; for ( int i = 2 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) { result *= i ; } return result ; }

s.h: The limits of the machine are part of the specification
s.x: Even Version 3 hides a subtle problem: arithmetic overflow . The factorial grows extremely fast: 12! = 479{,}001{,}600 fits in an int (maximum 2{,}147{,}483{,}647 ), but 13! = 6{,}227{,}020{,}800 does not. 20! = 2{,}432{,}902{,}008{,}176{,}640{,}000 fits in a long (maximum about 9.22 \times 10^{18} ), but 21! does not. In Java, integer overflow does not raise an error: the value silently wraps around and the method returns a wrong (sometimes even negative) number. That is why the specification of Section 3 restricted the domain to 0 \le n \le 20 . If we really need larger values, we must change the data representation (for example, using java.math.BigInteger ), which in turn changes the cost of each multiplication. This version is also iterative . The recursive versions need one stack frame per call, so their extra memory grows proportionally to n . The loop needs only a couple of variables, whatever the value of n . Both compute the same function, but they consume resources differently, an idea we will formalise when studying complexity. 🧠 Checkpoint: Tail calls and finiteness Question: Suppose we run the naive version in a language with tail call optimization (TCO), where certain recursive calls reuse the current stack frame instead of allocating a new one. Would TCO make the naive implementation correct for negative inputs? Answer: No. TCO might prevent the StackOverflowError , but it does not fix the logical problem: the control flow still never reaches a base case. The program would loop forever, consuming CPU time without producing an output. Finiteness is still violated, regardless of how the runtime manages the stack. (Incidentally, n * factorial(n - 1) is not even a tail call, because the multiplication happens after the recursive call returns.) 🧠 Checkpoint: Silent failures Question: Which is more dangerous in production: Version 1 called with n = -5 , or Version 3 called with n = 25 ? Answer: Probably Version 3 with n = 25 . Version 1 crashes loudly, so the error is noticed immediately. Version 3 returns a wrong number without any warning because of overflow, and that wrong value may be stored, displayed or used in later decisions. Silent failures are usually much harder to detect and diagnose than crashes.

The primary purpose of most programs is to store and retrieve information , and to transform it. To do so efficiently we need two things that cannot be separated: Data structures , which organize information in memory, and Algorithms , which operate on those structures. Niklaus Wirth, the creator of Pascal, summarized this idea in the title of his classic 1976 book: Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs . Choosing a good algorithm with an inappropriate data structure (or vice versa) usually leads to poor results. We will revisit this in the chapter dedicated to data structures. The goal of this course This course is about helping you understand how to structure information to support efficient processing in order to solve problems . Every chapter adds new tools to that same goal: analyzing the cost of a solution, and designing strategies that keep that cost under control.

Not all programming problems are equally challenging from an algorithmic point of view. Simple programming problems share three features: They can be solved with a linear scan : going through the data once. It is difficult to do better, because every element must be read at least once. The obvious approach works. Computing the sum of a list, its maximum element or the number of elements that satisfy a condition are typical examples. You can find implementations of the first two in the course repository ( sum and maximum ). Not-so-simple problems are different: It is not clear how to solve them at first sight. The simple ideas are too slow for realistic input sizes. They often require optimization : among many valid solutions, we want the best one. Finding the shortest route between two cities, scheduling exams so that no student has two at the same time, or packing the most valuable set of items into a limited space all belong to this second group. These are the problems that this course focuses on. 🧠 Checkpoint: Which kind of problem? Question: Which of the following problems is most representative of the problems this course focuses on? (a) find the median of a list of numbers, (b) find the first number of a list, (c) find the most interesting element of a list. Answer: (a), the median. Option (b) is trivial: it requires a single access. Option (c) is tempting, but it is not a computational problem at all : "most interesting" has no precise definition, so no algorithm can be correct or incorrect for it. Finding the median, on the other hand, is a well-defined problem where the obvious approach (sorting the whole list) works but is not optimal, and where clever algorithms do better. This is exactly the kind of problem we will study.

s.h: Two Goals When Designing a Solution
s.x: When we design a computer program, we typically pursue two goals that are sometimes in tension: To design an algorithm that is easy to understand, code and debug . To design an algorithm that makes an efficient use of the computer's resources . The ideal, of course, is to achieve both. The first goal is the main concern of other courses in your degree (software engineering, programming methodology, testing). This course focuses on the second goal , without forgetting the first: an efficient algorithm that nobody can understand or maintain is rarely a good engineering solution.

Two terms will appear throughout the course: The cost of a solution is the amount of resources it consumes. A solution is efficient if it solves the problem within the required resource constraints. Note that efficiency is relative to the constraints . A sorting program that takes ten seconds may be perfectly efficient for a nightly batch process and completely unacceptable for an interactive web page. Which resources can an algorithm consume? Execution time , the most commonly analyzed resource. Memory (space), both for the data and for auxiliary structures such as the call stack. Input/output and storage accesses , which can dominate the cost when data does not fit in main memory. Network communication , essential in distributed systems. Energy , increasingly important in mobile devices and data centers. Number of processors or cores , in parallel algorithms. In this course we will focus mainly on time and memory . As you will see in the case study of the next lesson, these two resources often compete: saving time may cost memory, and vice versa, so we will frequently look for a reasonable compromise.

s.h: How Can We Solve Complex Problems?
s.x: The universal strategy for dealing with complexity, in algorithms and in engineering in general, is decomposition : dividing the problem into subproblems so that: each subproblem is well detailed (it has its own precise specification), each subproblem can be solved independently , and the solutions of the subproblems can be combined into a solution of the original problem. At first, we do not need to know how each subproblem will be solved; we only need to know that it can be solved and what it guarantees. This is the concept of abstraction : we reason about a component through its contract, not through its internal details. For example, when we design an algorithm that needs a sorted list, we can simply assume a sort operation with a known cost, and worry about how to implement it later. Many of the algorithm design paradigms in this course are, in essence, different ways of decomposing a problem: Paradigm How the problem is decomposed Divide and conquer Into independent subproblems of the same kind, whose solutions are combined. Dynamic programming Into overlapping subproblems, whose solutions are stored to avoid recomputing them. Greedy algorithms Into a sequence of local decisions, each one taken and never undone. Backtracking Into a sequence of decisions explored systematically, undoing the ones that lead to dead ends. Branch and bound Like backtracking, but using estimates to explore the most promising options first and discard hopeless ones.

There is no general procedure for designing a good algorithm . There is no formula that, given any problem, produces the best algorithm for it. What exists is a collection of paradigms (like those in the table above), techniques for analyzing cost, and a large body of known algorithms that can be adapted. Aho, Hopcroft and Ullman, in their classic The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms (1974), put it this way: perhaps the most important principle for the good algorithm designer is to refuse to be content . The first solution that works is rarely the best one. Good designers keep asking: can I do better? Where is the time going? Is all this memory really necessary? The case study in the next lesson follows exactly this attitude, improving a solution step by step.

Algorithms are no longer confined to textbooks and servers: they make decisions that affect people's lives every day. A quick look at news headlines from recent years shows the variety: Recommendation and entertainment. In 2009, Netflix awarded a one-million-dollar prize to a team of researchers ( BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos ) for improving the accuracy of its movie recommendation algorithm. Streaming platforms also use algorithms to estimate how much a piece of content is worth. Science and health. Algorithms compete to predict the structure of proteins (a field in which DeepMind's AlphaFold achieved a historic breakthrough) and to help design personalised cancer vaccines. Safety-critical systems. Aircraft, drones and medical devices are controlled by algorithms. News reports have attributed crashes of military drones to poor software design, a reminder that an algorithmic error can destroy expensive equipment or put lives at risk. Society and fairness. Translation systems have reproduced gender stereotypes, content moderation algorithms have flagged harmless publications, changes to social network feeds have influenced which news people see, and automatic pricing has raised the cost of products during emergencies. Perception. Computer vision algorithms now match or surpass human performance on some image recognition tasks. These examples show that the properties studied in this chapter are not academic details. Correctness matters because a wrong answer can have real consequences. Efficiency matters because many of these systems process billions of items. And, increasingly, we also ask algorithms to be fair, transparent and explainable , so that people can understand and question the decisions that affect them.

Algorithmic questions are a standard part of technical interviews for software development positions. Many classic interview questions correspond directly to topics in this course: Typical interview question Where you will study it Sort a sequence of elements under some rule (for example, without nested loops). Sorting algorithms; divide and conquer (Mergesort, Quicksort). Compute the n -th Fibonacci number, usually recursively. Recursion; divide and conquer; dynamic programming. Solve the Towers of Hanoi with n discs. Recursion; divide and conquer. Solve a Sudoku. Backtracking. Escape from a maze in the minimum number of steps. Backtracking; branch and bound; graph search. Solve a sliding puzzle (such as the 15-puzzle). Branch and bound. Maximize the value carried in a backpack with a weight limit (knapsack problem). Greedy algorithms; dynamic programming; backtracking; branch and bound. Interviewers also ask conceptual questions, such as: What is an algorithm? What is the time complexity of an algorithm? What is the space complexity of Insertion sort? What is the difference between the best and the worst case? How does Quicksort work? What is asymptotic analysis? What are the main approaches to designing algorithms? By the end of this course, you should be able to answer all of them with confidence. What interviewers really evaluate In an algorithmic interview, the final code is only part of the evaluation. Interviewers want to see whether you clarify the problem (input domain, edge cases), start from a correct solution, analyze its cost and then improve it . In other words, they evaluate algorithmic thinking, exactly the skill this course is designed to develop.

Studying algorithmics is not about memorizing a catalog of programming tricks. It is about internalising a way of thinking that remains valuable as languages, frameworks and platforms change. It is important for all branches of computer science. Databases, operating systems, networks, compilers, graphics, artificial intelligence and security all rely on efficient algorithms and data structures. It plays a key role in technological innovation. Search engines, route planners, compression formats, cryptography and machine learning are, at their core, algorithmic achievements. It is independent of languages and tools. Today's Java, Python or Rust will evolve or be replaced, but the reasons why one strategy scales better than another remain valid across languages, compilers and hardware generations. It helps you think about how to solve problems. Algorithmic thinking trains you to look past variable names and syntax and focus on the structure of the problem: what needs to be computed and how its cost grows. It lets you evaluate designs before building them. By analyzing how a strategy behaves as the input grows, you can detect bottlenecks early and compare alternatives on paper, instead of discovering the problem after months of development. It is challenging, and good for the brain. Designing an elegant algorithm is an intellectual exercise that combines creativity and rigour.

The word algorithm derives from al-Khwarizmi; its meaning evolved from decimal arithmetic to any precise, mechanical problem-solving procedure. An algorithm solves a problem , defined by a specification (precondition and postcondition) that applies to all its instances . Knuth's five properties ( finiteness, definiteness, input, output and effectiveness ) form the minimal contract of an algorithm. Code that works on a few examples is not necessarily an algorithm: the factorial shows how domain checks, error handling and machine limits (overflow, stack size) are part of the design. This course focuses on efficiency : solving problems within resource constraints, mainly time and memory. Complex problems are tackled through decomposition and abstraction , the basis of the design paradigms of the course. There is no universal recipe for designing algorithms: good designers refuse to be content with their first solution.

💻 Explore the code. The course repository ( documentation and source code ) contains the factorial examples of this lesson in src/topics/foundation/factorial . Run the unsafe version with a negative argument and observe the StackOverflowError . 🔬 Experiment with the stack. Run the recursive factorial with large values of n and change the stack size of the JVM with the -Xss option (for example, -Xss256k and -Xss8m ). How does the maximum recursion depth change? Does the iterative version care? 🧮 Find the overflow. Write a loop that prints n! for n = 0, 1, \dots, 25 using int , then long . Identify the exact point where each type overflows and compare with the values given in Version 4. Then repeat the experiment using Math.multiplyExact , which throws an exception instead of overflowing silently. ✍️ Write specifications. Write a precondition and a postcondition for: (a) Euclid's algorithm; (b) finding the maximum of a list; (c) finding the position of an element in a list. In (c), what should happen if the element appears twice? And if it does not appear at all?

t: Asymptotic Notation: Describing How Cost Grows

s.x: ⏱ 14 min read Read first: Complexity Analysis In the previous lesson we obtained exact expressions such as T(n) = 3n + 4 and saw that the constants depend on arbitrary counting decisions and, in reality, on the machine. What does not depend on them is the rate of growth of the function: how fast T(n) increases when n becomes large. Asymptotic notation is the mathematical language for describing that rate of growth. It refers to the speed of growth of the values of a function f(n) as n tends to infinity, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. It is the notation used in every textbook, paper and technical interview to talk about the efficiency of algorithms. What you will learn in this lesson The formal definition of O (big-O) and how to prove that a function belongs to O(f(n)) . The related notations \Omega (big-Omega) and \Theta (big-Theta), and what each one really says. The algebraic properties that let us simplify expressions without going back to the definition. The logarithm rules you need for analyzing algorithms, and why the base of a logarithm does not matter. How to determine the order of complex expressions quickly and reliably.

s.h: Big-O: An Upper Bound on Growth
s.x: Definition. A function T(n) is O(f(n)) if there exist two positive constants c and n_0 such that: T(n) \le c \cdot f(n) \qquad \text{for all } n \ge n_0 In words: from some point n_0 onwards, T(n) never exceeds a constant multiple of f(n) . If T(n) is O(f(n)) , we say that T(n) has, at most , a growth rate of f(n) . The definition of Big-O in a picture. Before n₀ anything can happen; from n₀ onwards, T(n) never rises above the curve c · f(n). Two details of the definition are important: The constant c absorbs the constant factors: 3n , 100n and n/2 are all O(n) . This is exactly the freedom we need, since constants depend on the machine and on the counting conventions. The threshold n_0 means that only the behavior for large values of n matters. What happens for small inputs is irrelevant to the definition.

Let us prove that T(n) = 5n^4 + 4n^3 is O(n^4) . We need constants c and n_0 such that 5n^4 + 4n^3 \le c \cdot n^4 for every n \ge n_0 . The idea is to bound the lower-order term by the dominant one. For n \ge 4 we have 4n^3 \le n \cdot n^3 = n^4 , therefore: 5n^4 + 4n^3 \le 5n^4 + n^4 = 6n^4 \qquad \text{for all } n \ge 4 So the definition holds with c = 6 and n_0 = 4 (or any larger n_0 , such as n_0 = 5 ). The values of c and n_0 are not unique: with c = 9 , for example, the inequality holds from n_0 = 1 , because 4n^3 \le 4n^4 for n \ge 1 . We only need to show that some pair exists. A quicker test with limits When the limit exists, we can compare growth rates with: \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{T(n)}{f(n)} = L If L is a finite number (including 0), then T(n) is O(f(n)) . If L = 0 , T(n) grows strictly more slowly than f(n) . If L is a finite positive number, both functions grow at the same rate . If L = \infty , T(n) grows faster, and it is not O(f(n)) . For example, \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{5n^4 + 4n^3}{n^4} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(5 + \frac{4}{n}\right) = 5 , so both functions grow at the same rate.

s.h: Big-O is a bound, not an exact description
s.x: Since O is an upper bound, a function belongs to many classes: 3n + 4 is O(n) , but also O(n^2) and O(2^n) , because all those functions grow at least as fast as n . These statements are true but not very informative. When we analyze an algorithm, we always give the tightest bound we can prove: saying that the sum of a vector is O(n^2) is correct, but misleading. Big-O does not mean "worst case" A common misconception is that O describes the worst case. It does not: O , \Omega and \Theta describe functions , and any of the functions we studied in the previous lesson can be described with them. The worst-case time of linear search is O(n) , its best-case time is O(1) , its average-case time is O(n) . When someone says that "an algorithm is O(n^2) " without further detail, they usually mean that its worst-case time is O(n^2) , but the two ideas are independent.

Big-O gives an upper bound. Two related notations complete the picture: \Omega (big-Omega), a lower bound. T(n) is \Omega(f(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n_0 such that T(n) \ge c \cdot f(n) for all n \ge n_0 . It says that T(n) grows at least as fast as f(n) . \Theta (big-Theta), an exact order. T(n) is \Theta(f(n)) if it is both O(f(n)) and \Omega(f(n)) , that is, if there exist positive constants c_1 , c_2 and n_0 such that c_1 \cdot f(n) \le T(n) \le c_2 \cdot f(n) for all n \ge n_0 . It says that T(n) grows exactly at the rate of f(n) , up to constants. Notation Meaning Analogy Example T(n) \in O(f(n)) grows at most as fast as f(n) \le 3n + 4 \in O(n^2) (true, but not tight) T(n) \in \Omega(f(n)) grows at least as fast as f(n) \ge 3n + 4 \in \Omega(n) T(n) \in \Theta(f(n)) grows exactly as fast as f(n) = 3n + 4 \in \Theta(n) These notations also allow us to talk about problems , not only algorithms. For example, we saw in the case study that any algorithm for the maximum pairwise product must read all the elements, so every algorithm for that problem takes \Omega(n) time in the worst case. Since the linear scan is O(n) , it is optimal : no algorithm can have a better growth rate. Lower bounds are what allow us to measure the inherent difficulty of a problem . Notation in practice In everyday use (and in this course), people often write O when they actually mean \Theta : "the sum of a vector is O(n) " is usually intended as "it grows exactly linearly". Also, although O(f(n)) is formally a set of functions, you will commonly see T(n) = O(f(n)) instead of T(n) \in O(f(n)) . Read the " = " as "is", not as a true equality: n = O(n^2) is correct, but O(n^2) = n makes no sense.

s.h: Why Constants Can Be Ignored (and When They Matter)
s.x: With asymptotic notation, we can evaluate a program by its growth rate, ignoring constants: a program that is O(n) will be better than one that is O(n^2) for large enough inputs . However, there are values of n for which an algorithm with time 100n behaves worse than one with time n^2 : as long as n \lt 100 , n^2 is smaller than 100n . Asymptotic notation guarantees that the linear algorithm wins eventually, not that it wins for every input size. In practice: For large inputs , the growth rate is decisive, and the constants become irrelevant. For small inputs , constants can matter, and a "worse" algorithm may be faster. This is why, for example, efficient sorting libraries often switch to a simple quadratic algorithm (insertion sort) for very small subarrays. To facilitate the analysis, the values of the constants are usually removed. But a good engineer remembers that they exist.

The following properties allow us to simplify expressions without returning to the definition every time: Reflexivity. T(n) is O(T(n)) . Every function is a bound of itself (take c = 1 ). Constant factors. O(c \cdot f(n)) = O(f(n)) for any constant c \gt 0 . Multiplying by a constant does not change the class. Sum rule. If T(n) = T_1(n) + T_2(n) + \cdots + T_m(n) , with m fixed, then T(n) is of the order of the largest term: O(\max(T_1(n), T_2(n), \dots, T_m(n))) . This is the rule for sequential code: the slowest part dominates. Product rule. If T(n) = T_1(n) \cdot T_2(n) \cdots T_m(n) , then T(n) is O(T_1(n) \cdot T_2(n) \cdots T_m(n)) . This is the rule for nested code: a loop of O(n) iterations whose body costs O(n) is O(n^2) . Base of logarithms. O(\log_a n) = O(\log_b n) = O(\log n) for any bases a, b \gt 1 . Powers inside a logarithm. O(\log(n^k)) = O(k \log n) = O(\log n) for any constant k . Powers of a logarithm. O(\log^k n) \ne O(\log n) for k \gt 1 . Here \log^k n means (\log n)^k , which grows faster than \log n . Properties 5, 6 and 7 deserve a closer look, because logarithms appear constantly in algorithm analysis.

s.h: Why the base of the logarithm does not matter
s.x: The change-of-base formula says that, for any bases a, b \gt 1 : \log_a n = \frac{\log_b n}{\log_b a} = \frac{1}{\log_b a} \cdot \log_b n Since \frac{1}{\log_b a} is a constant , logarithms in different bases differ only by a constant factor, and property 2 tells us that constant factors do not change the class. That is why we simply write O(\log n) . In computing, when a base is needed, it is usually 2, because many algorithms halve the problem at each step.

Compare \log(n^8) and (\log n)^8 : \log(n^8) = 8 \log n , which is just a constant times \log n , so it is O(\log n) (property 6). (\log n)^8 is the logarithm raised to the eighth power. It grows faster than any constant times \log n , so it is not O(\log n) (property 7). It is still much smaller than any power of n : even (\log n)^8 is eventually smaller than \sqrt{n} , although only for very large n . ∴ Proof Rules of the big O notation → ∴ Proof Logarithms grow more slowly than any power →

These identities, valid for positive values and bases different from 1, are used continuously when analyzing algorithms: \log_a(n^k) = k \cdot \log_a n \log_a(n \cdot m) = \log_a n + \log_a m \log_a(n / m) = \log_a n - \log_a m n^{\log_a b} = b^{\log_a n} \log_a b \cdot \log_b n = \log_a n Rule 4 is less familiar but very useful, especially in divide and conquer: it allows us to convert an expression like 3^{\log_2 n} into n^{\log_2 3} \approx n^{1.585} . You can prove it by taking \log_a of both sides: both become \log_a n \cdot \log_a b .

🧠 Is n^{\log_3 a} = a^{\log_3 n} ? Yes. It is rule 4 with base 3. Taking \log_3 of both sides gives \log_3 a \cdot \log_3 n in both cases. 🧠 Is O(\log_3 (n^8)) = O(8 \log_3 n) ? And O((\log_3 n)^8) = O(8 \log_3 n) ? The first one, yes : by rule 1, \log_3(n^8) = 8 \log_3 n , and both are O(\log n) . The second one, no : (\log_3 n)^8 is a power of the logarithm and grows faster than \log n (property 7). Always pay attention to whether the exponent applies to n or to the logarithm. 🧠 Is \log_3(4n) = \log_3 4 \cdot \log_3 n ? No. The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms (rule 2): \log_3(4n) = \log_3 4 + \log_3 n . Asymptotically, it is still O(\log n) , because \log_3 4 is just a constant added to \log_3 n . 🧠 Is \log_3 4 \cdot \log_4 n = \log_3 n ? Yes. It is rule 5 with a = 3 and b = 4 , a form of the change-of-base formula.

s.h: Determining the Order of an Expression
s.x: In practice, finding the order of an expression consists of identifying its dominant term and dropping its constant factor. To identify the dominant term, it helps to remember the order of growth of the most common functions, from slowest to fastest: 1 \;\lt\; \log n \;\lt\; \log^2 n \;\lt\; \sqrt{n} \;\lt\; n \;\lt\; n \log n \;\lt\; n^2 \;\lt\; n^3 \;\lt\; 2^n \;\lt\; n! \;\lt\; n^n and two general facts: Any power of n (even a tiny one, such as n^{0.1} ) eventually grows faster than any power of \log n . Any exponential c^n with c \gt 1 eventually grows faster than any polynomial n^k . The following examples apply these ideas. Cover the "Order" column and try to find the order of each expression yourself; the "Why?" tab explains the ones that hide a trap. Examples (I) Examples (II) Why? T(n) Order \frac{4}{5} n^3 + 100 O(n^3) 10 n \log n O(n \log n) 100n + \frac{3}{10000} n \log n O(n \log n) 2\sqrt{n} + n^2 + 50n O(n^2) n \log n + 2n + 13 O(n \log n) n^2 + 4(n + \log n)^2 \cdot n O(n^3) \frac{4n^2 + 2 \log n}{n + 1} O(n) 16 \log n + n^{0.4} O(n^{0.4}) T(n) Order n^3 + 1005n O(n^3) 3n^2 + 59n O(n^2) \frac{1}{10} \cdot 2^n + 4n^2 O(2^n) 5n^{1.6} + 10 n \log n O(n^{1.6}) n \log n + 10^4 n + 10^{100} O(n \log n) 2^n + 4(n + \log n)^2 \cdot n O(2^n) Some of these examples contain a trap: 100n + \frac{3}{10000} n \log n : the coefficient of n \log n is tiny and the coefficient of n is large, but n \log n still grows faster. Constants never change the class; they only change when the dominant term takes over (here, for astronomically large n ). n^2 + 4(n + \log n)^2 \cdot n : expanding (n + \log n)^2 = n^2 + 2n \log n + \log^2 n and multiplying by n gives a dominant term 4n^3 . \frac{4n^2 + 2 \log n}{n + 1} : for large n , this behaves like \frac{4n^2}{n} = 4n . 16 \log n + n^{0.4} : even a small power of n beats a logarithm. n \log n + 10^4 n + 10^{100} : the constant 10^{100} is enormous, but it is still a constant. 5n^{1.6} + 10 n \log n : compare n^{1.6} with n \log n by dividing both by n : n^{0.6} grows faster than \log n . 🧠 Checkpoint: Order these functions Question: Order these functions by increasing growth rate: n^3 , \log_2 n , n^{0.5} , 2^n , n \log_2 n , \log_{10} n , n^2 / \log n , n^{1.01} , n! . Answer: \log_2 n and \log_{10} n (same order; they differ only by a constant factor) \lt n^{0.5} \lt n \log_2 n \lt n^{1.01} \lt n^2 / \log n \lt n^3 \lt 2^n \lt n! . The most delicate pair is n \log n versus n^{1.01} : dividing both by n , we compare \log n with n^{0.01} , and any power of n eventually beats the logarithm. However, the crossover happens for an astronomically large n , so for any practical input size, n \log n is the smaller of the two.

Asymptotic notation describes the growth rate of a function, ignoring constant factors and the behavior for small n . T(n) \in O(f(n)) means T(n) \le c \cdot f(n) from some n_0 onwards: an upper bound . \Omega is a lower bound and \Theta an exact order . Asymptotic bounds and the best, worst and average cases are independent ideas. Lower bounds on problems let us prove that an algorithm is optimal . Key properties: constants are dropped, a sum is dominated by its largest term, products multiply, and the base of logarithms is irrelevant, but powers of logarithms are not. To find the order of an expression, identify the dominant term using the hierarchy of functions.

✍️ Prove it. Using the definition, find constants c and n_0 that prove that 3n^2 + 59n is O(n^2) . Then prove that it is also \Omega(n^2) , and conclude that it is \Theta(n^2) . ❌ Disprove it. Show that n^2 is not O(n) . (Hint: assume that constants c and n_0 exist and find an n \ge n_0 that breaks the inequality.) 🔁 Logarithms. Simplify 2^{\log_2 n} , 4^{\log_2 n} and n^{\log_n 2} . Which of them grow polynomially? 📊 Visualize. Plot 100n , n^2 and n \log_2 n for n between 1 and 200 (with a spreadsheet or any plotting tool). Where does each curve overtake the others? 🎯 Tight bounds. For each of the methods you analyzed in the previous lesson (maximum of a vector, checking if a vector is sorted), give the tightest bound for the best and the worst case.

⏱ 20 min read Read first: Algorithmic Thinking To truly understand why algorithmics matters, it helps to experience failure first. In this case study we take a deceptively simple problem and solve it again and again. Each version fixes a problem of the previous one, and each fix teaches a different lesson: about the limits of data types, the cost of naive strategies, the impact of data representation, and the danger of "optimizations" that are not actually correct. This is exactly the attitude described in the previous lesson: a good algorithm designer refuses to be content with the first solution that works. What you will learn in this lesson How to state a problem precisely and check your understanding with small examples. Why arithmetic overflow happens, why it is silent in Java, and how to avoid it correctly. How the number of operations of a brute-force solution grows, and why faster hardware does not fix it. How sorting and, finally, a single linear scan reduce the cost from quadratic to linear time. How data representation affects memory consumption. How to gain confidence in a fast algorithm using stress testing , and how a plausible-looking optimization can be wrong.

Objective: given a sequence of non-negative integers, find the maximum product that can be obtained by multiplying two elements located at different positions of the sequence. Formal specification: Input: a sequence A = [a_0, a_1, \dots, a_{n-1}] of non-negative integers, with n \ge 2 . Output: the value \max \{\, a_i \cdot a_j : 0 \le i, j \le n-1,\; i \ne j \,\} . Before writing any code, it is good practice to solve a few small instances by hand. This checks that we understand the problem and gives us test cases for later: For [7, 3, 6] the possible products are 7 \cdot 3 = 21 , 7 \cdot 6 = 42 and 3 \cdot 6 = 18 , so the answer is 42 . For [5, 5] the answer is 25 . The two factors may have the same value , as long as they are at different positions . This detail, which is easy to overlook, will matter later. For [0, 9] the answer is 0 : with only two elements there is only one possible pair. Read the specification carefully "Two distinct elements" is ambiguous in everyday language: distinct values or distinct positions? The formal specification ( i \ne j ) removes the ambiguity. Many bugs come from implementing the problem we think we read instead of the one that was actually specified.

s.h: Step 1: Two Numbers and the Primitive Type Trap
s.x: Let us start with the simplest possible instance: just two numbers, 100,000 and 1,000,000 . The expected result is 10^{11} = 100{,}000{,}000{,}000 . public class MaxPairWiseProduct { private final int operandA = 100_000 ; private final int operandB = 1_000_000 ; public int compute ( ) { return operandA * operandB ; } } If we run it, the program prints 1215752192 . No exception, no warning: just a wrong number. Arithmetic overflow The Java type int uses 32 bits and can represent values in the range [-2^{31}, 2^{31}-1] , that is, up to 2{,}147{,}483{,}647 . When the true result of an operation does not fit, Java keeps only the lowest 32 bits of the result. Mathematically, the value is reduced modulo 2^{32} and interpreted in two's complement: 10^{11} \bmod 2^{32} = 1{,}215{,}752{,}192 The result is not random: it is completely deterministic. But it is wrong, and nothing tells us so. Depending on the operands, the "wrapped" value can even be negative. The size of the primitive types is part of the language specification (unlike in C or C++, where it may depend on the platform): Type Size Range byte 8 bits -128 to 127 short 16 bits -32{,}768 to 32{,}767 int 32 bits about \pm 2.1 \times 10^{9} long 64 bits about \pm 9.2 \times 10^{18} Java implementation in the course repository vicegd/algorithms · package topics.foundation.maxpairwise J MaxPairWiseProduct.java ↗

s.h: Step 2: Moving to long , and a Second Trap
s.x: The obvious fix is to use 64-bit integers, which can store values up to about 9.22 \times 10^{18} : private final long operandA = 100_000L ; private final long operandB = 1_000_000L ; public long compute ( ) { return operandA * operandB ; // 100000000000, correct } This works. However, in real programs the inputs usually arrive as int values (for example, read from a file or stored in an int[] ), and a very common mistake is to change only the type of the variable that stores the result: int a = 100_000 , b = 1_000_000 ; long wrong = a * b ; // 1215752192: the multiplication is still done in 32 bits! long right = ( long ) a * b ; // 100000000000: a is promoted to long BEFORE multiplying In a * b , both operands are int , so Java performs a 32-bit multiplication, overflows, and only then converts the already wrong result to long . Casting one of the operands forces a 64-bit multiplication. Is long always enough? For this problem, yes. If the inputs are int values, each one is at most 2^{31}-1 , so any product is at most (2^{31}-1)^2 \approx 4.6 \times 10^{18} , which is below the maximum long value ( 2^{63}-1 \approx 9.22 \times 10^{18} ). This is a small example of reasoning about the whole input domain instead of trusting a few tests. When you cannot bound the values like this, use Math.multiplyExact(a, b) , which throws an ArithmeticException instead of overflowing silently, or java.math.BigInteger for arbitrary precision. Lesson 1: always respect the physical limits of your data types, and remember that in most languages overflow is silent. Java implementation in the course repository vicegd/algorithms · package topics.foundation.maxpairwise J MaxPairWiseProduct2.java ↗

Two numbers are not an interesting instance. Let us create a realistic dataset: 100,000 random integers between 0 and 99 , written to a text file so that every version of our algorithm works with exactly the same data. public static void main ( String . . . args ) throws IOException { Path path = Paths . get ( "MaxPairWiseProductRandomNumbers.txt" ) ; Random random = new Random ( ) ; try ( BufferedWriter writer = Files . newBufferedWriter ( path ) ) { for ( int i = 0 ; i < 100_000 ; i ++ ) { writer . write ( random . nextInt ( 100 ) + " " ) ; } } } Each version then reads the file into a list in its constructor: private final List < Integer > numbers = new ArrayList < > ( ) ; public MaxPairWiseProduct3 ( ) { Path path = Paths . get ( "MaxPairWiseProductRandomNumbers.txt" ) ; try ( BufferedReader reader = Files . newBufferedReader ( path ) ) { for ( String number : reader . readLine ( ) . split ( " " ) ) { numbers . add ( Integer . valueOf ( number ) ) ; } } catch ( IOException e ) { // log the error } } 🧠 Checkpoint: Predict the answer Question: Before running any algorithm, what result do you expect for this dataset? Answer: Almost certainly 99 \cdot 99 = 9801 . With 100,000 values uniformly distributed between 0 and 99, the value 99 is expected to appear about 1,000 times, so it is practically certain that it appears at least twice, at two different positions. Predicting the result is a cheap and useful sanity check for any program. Java implementation in the course repository vicegd/algorithms · package topics.foundation.maxpairwise J MaxPairWiseProductRandomNumbers.java ↗

The most direct strategy follows the specification literally: try every pair of positions (i, j) with i \ne j , compute the product and keep the largest. public long compute ( ) { long maxProduct = 0 ; for ( int i = 0 ; i < numbers . size ( ) ; i ++ ) { for ( int j = 0 ; j < numbers . size ( ) ; j ++ ) { if ( i != j ) { long result = ( long ) numbers . get ( i ) * numbers . get ( j ) ; if ( result > maxProduct ) { maxProduct = result ; } } } } return maxProduct ; } This algorithm is correct : it examines all candidate pairs, so it cannot miss the best one. Its problem is cost .

The inner body is executed n \cdot n = n^2 times (and the product is computed n(n-1) times). For n = 100{,}000 that is 10^{10} iterations: ten thousand million. A first improvement is to notice that a_i \cdot a_j = a_j \cdot a_i , so each pair only needs to be checked once. Starting the inner loop at j = i + 1 also makes the i != j test unnecessary: for ( int i = 0 ; i < numbers . size ( ) ; i ++ ) for ( int j = i + 1 ; j < numbers . size ( ) ; j ++ ) . . . Now the body runs \frac{n(n-1)}{2} times, about 5 \times 10^9 for our dataset. We have halved the work, which is welcome, but the shape of the growth has not changed: it is still proportional to n^2 .

The following times were measured on one machine, with an int[] version of these algorithms and the JIT compiler enabled. The exact numbers will be different on your computer; what matters is how they grow: n All pairs ( n^2 ) Half of the pairs ( n^2/2 ) 10,000 0.08 s 0.06 s 20,000 0.22 s 0.07 s 40,000 0.89 s 0.29 s 100,000 5.8 s 1.8 s Look at the left column: when n doubles from 20,000 to 40,000, the time is multiplied by about 4 . When n grows 2.5 times (from 40,000 to 100,000), the time grows about 2.5^2 \approx 6.25 times. This is the signature of quadratic growth . Extrapolating, one million numbers would take around ten minutes, and ten million numbers around 16 hours. The limits of hardware A quadratic algorithm cannot be rescued by buying a faster processor. A machine that is twice as fast lets you process, in the same time, an input only \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41 times larger. Doubling the input still quadruples the time, whatever the hardware. 🧠 Checkpoint: Faster CPU or better algorithm? Question: Your quadratic program takes one hour for a certain input. You can either buy a CPU that is 4 times faster, or replace the algorithm with one whose time grows linearly. Which option lets you process a 100 times larger input in about one hour? Answer: Only the better algorithm. With the faster CPU, a 100 times larger input needs 100^2 = 10{,}000 times more work, which takes 10{,}000 / 4 = 2{,}500 hours. A linear algorithm only needs 100 times more work than it needed for the original input, and for large inputs a linear algorithm is usually far faster than the quadratic one to begin with. Lesson 2: a correct algorithm can still be useless if its cost grows too fast. We need a better strategy, not a faster machine. Java implementation in the course repository vicegd/algorithms · package topics.foundation.maxpairwise J MaxPairWiseProduct3.java ↗

Brute force wastes most of its time multiplying small numbers that can never produce the maximum. The key observation is: Since all numbers are non-negative, the maximum product is always obtained by multiplying the two largest elements. (If x \ge y are the two largest values, any other pair a_i \cdot a_j satisfies a_i \le x and a_j \le y for a suitable ordering of the pair, so a_i \cdot a_j \le x \cdot y .) A natural way of finding the two largest elements is to sort the data. Sorting in descending order places them in the first two positions: public long compute ( ) { if ( numbers . size ( ) < 2 ) throw new IllegalStateException ( "At least two numbers are required" ) ; numbers . sort ( Collections . reverseOrder ( ) ) ; // largest first long candidate1 = numbers . get ( 0 ) ; long candidate2 = numbers . get ( 1 ) ; return candidate1 * candidate2 ; } (An equivalent formulation is to sort in ascending order with Collections.sort and then reverse the list with Collections.reverse .) Good sorting algorithms need a number of operations proportional to n \log_2 n , as you will see in the sorting chapter. For n = 100{,}000 that is about 1.7 \times 10^6 basic steps instead of 5 \times 10^9 . In our measurements, the time drops from seconds to a few milliseconds : more than a thousand times faster than the all-pairs brute force. A side effect This version modifies the caller's data : after calling compute() , the list is sorted. If other parts of the program relied on the original order, we have introduced a bug that has nothing to do with the maximum product. When an algorithm needs to reorder its input, it should either document it clearly or work on a copy (which costs extra memory). Java implementation in the course repository vicegd/algorithms · package topics.foundation.maxpairwise J MaxPairWiseProduct4.java ↗

Do we need the descending order (or the extra pass to reverse the list)? No. After an ascending sort, the two largest elements are simply at the end: public long compute ( ) { if ( numbers . size ( ) < 2 ) throw new IllegalStateException ( "At least two numbers are required" ) ; Collections . sort ( numbers ) ; // ascending long candidate1 = numbers . get ( numbers . size ( ) - 1 ) ; long candidate2 = numbers . get ( numbers . size ( ) - 2 ) ; return candidate1 * candidate2 ; } Asymptotically, nothing has changed: the cost is still dominated by the sort, proportional to n \log n . But we have removed work that was not needed (a custom comparator or a full reversal of the list). This illustrates a distinction that we will formalise in the next lessons: improvements that change the growth rate of the cost (from n^2 to n \log n ), which are decisive for large inputs, and improvements that only change the constant factors (doing the same kind of work, but less of it), which are useful but secondary. Java implementation in the course repository vicegd/algorithms · package topics.foundation.maxpairwise J MaxPairWiseProduct5.java ↗

Sorting rearranges all the elements, but we only need two of them. Can we find the two largest elements without sorting ? Yes, with a single pass over the data, keeping track of the largest and the second largest values seen so far: public long compute ( ) { if ( numbers . size ( ) < 2 ) throw new IllegalStateException ( "At least two numbers are required" ) ; long max1 = - 1 ; // largest value seen so far long max2 = - 1 ; // second largest value seen so far for ( int current : numbers ) { if ( current > max1 ) { max2 = max1 ; // the previous maximum becomes the second max1 = current ; // new maximum } else if ( current > max2 ) { max2 = current ; // not the largest, but beats the second } } return max1 * max2 ; } Let us trace it with [5, 3, 5] : Element Comparison max1 max2 (start) -1 -1 5 5 > -1 : new maximum 5 -1 3 3 \le 5 , 3 > -1 : new second 5 3 5 5 \le 5 , 5 > 3 : new second 5 5 The result is 5 \cdot 5 = 25 , which is correct: the two 5s are at different positions. Note that the second 5 goes to max2 precisely because the first comparison uses a strict > . This algorithm: reads each element exactly once , so its time is proportional to n ( linear ); uses only two extra variables, whatever the size of the input ( constant extra memory ); does not modify the input. In our measurements, it processes the 100,000 numbers in about a tenth of a millisecond , roughly 30 times faster than sorting and tens of thousands of times faster than brute force. And it is optimal in an important sense: any correct algorithm must read every element at least once (an unread element could be the largest), so no algorithm can grow more slowly than linearly. Java implementation in the course repository vicegd/algorithms · package topics.foundation.maxpairwise J MaxPairWiseProduct6.java ↗ ∴ Proof The linear maximum pairwise product is correct →

So far we have focused on time, but an efficient solution must also take care of memory consumption . There are two sources of memory use to consider. 1. Auxiliary memory of the algorithm. Brute force and the linear scan need only a few variables. Sorting a list of objects in Java, on the other hand, uses an algorithm (TimSort) that may need temporary space for up to about n/2 elements, that is, memory proportional to n . (Sorting an int[] with Arrays.sort uses a variant of Quicksort that works almost in place.) If we sort a copy to avoid the side effect described in Step 5, we need yet another n elements. 2. Representation of the data. All the versions store the numbers in a List<Integer> . In Java, a list cannot hold primitive values, so each number is stored as an Integer object: a reference in the list plus an object in the heap (typically around 16 bytes) for each element. An int[] stores each number in exactly 4 bytes, contiguously in memory, which is also friendlier to the processor cache. int [ ] numbers = new int [ 100_000 ] ; // about 400 KB of data A curiosity: the Integer cache Java keeps a cache of Integer objects for small values (by default, from -128 to 127 ). Since our numbers are between 0 and 99, Integer.valueOf always returns cached objects, and the list stores only references. With larger values, every element would be a separate object, and the list would need several times more memory than an int[] . Measuring memory in a managed language is full of subtleties like this one. Strategy Growth of the time Extra memory Modifies the input Time for n = 10^5 (measured) Brute force, all pairs n^2 constant no ≈ 5.8 s Brute force, half of the pairs n^2 constant no ≈ 1.8 s Sorting n \log n proportional to n yes (unless copied) ≈ 3.6 ms Linear scan n constant no ≈ 0.1 ms Lesson 3: efficiency is about all the resources. The best solution here wins in time, in memory and in side effects.

s.h: Is the Fast Version Really Correct? Stress Testing
s.x: Fast algorithms are usually more subtle than slow ones, and subtle code hides subtle bugs. Consider this version, which looks perfectly reasonable: first find the maximum, then find the largest value that is different from it. public static long buggyMaxPairwise ( int [ ] a ) { int max1 = - 1 ; for ( int x : a ) if ( x > max1 ) max1 = x ; int max2 = - 1 ; for ( int x : a ) if ( x != max1 && x > max2 ) max2 = x ; // BUG return ( long ) max1 * max2 ; } It passes the obvious tests: [7, 3, 6] gives 42, [1, 2, 3, 4] gives 12. But it excludes the maximum by value , not by position . For [5, 5] it computes 5 \cdot (-1) = -5 instead of 25, and on our dataset (where 99 appears about 1,000 times) it would return 99 \cdot 98 = 9702 instead of 9801. How can we find such bugs systematically? A powerful technique is stress testing : Keep a simple, obviously correct (even if slow) implementation: the brute force. Generate thousands of small random inputs . Run both implementations on each input and compare the results. As soon as they differ, print the input: it is a counterexample that you can debug by hand. Random random = new Random ( ) ; for ( int test = 0 ; test < 100_000 ; test ++ ) { int n = 2 + random . nextInt ( 8 ) ; // small sizes: 2..9 int [ ] a = new int [ n ] ; for ( int i = 0 ; i < n ; i ++ ) a [ i ] = random . nextInt ( 10 ) ; // small values: 0..9 long expected = bruteForce ( a ) ; long actual = buggyMaxPairwise ( a ) ; if ( expected != actual ) { System . out . println ( "Counterexample: " + Arrays . toString ( a ) + " expected " + expected + " but got " + actual ) ; break ; } } When we ran it (with a fixed random seed), it found a counterexample in the very first test: [3, 8, 4, 0, 5, 5, 8] , where the correct answer is 8 \cdot 8 = 64 but the buggy version returns 8 \cdot 5 = 40 . The same stress test, applied to the sorting and linear versions, found no differences in 100,000 random tests. Why small inputs? Random small inputs with small values are best: repeated values (like the two 8s above) appear frequently, and when a test fails, the counterexample is short enough to analyze by hand. Then complement random tests with deliberate edge cases : the minimum size ( n = 2 ), all elements equal, zeros, the maximum allowed values (to detect overflow) and the largest input sizes (to detect performance problems). Remember that testing, even stress testing, can show the presence of bugs but not their absence. For the linear scan we also have an argument : after processing each element, max1 and max2 hold the two largest values (counting repetitions) among the elements processed so far. This statement, which remains true after every iteration, is a loop invariant , a tool that you will meet again when reasoning about the correctness of algorithms. Lesson 4: an optimization is only an improvement if it is still correct. Keep the slow version: it is your best oracle.

s.h: Going Further: What If Negative Numbers Are Allowed?
s.x: Our specification said non-negative integers. Let us change it: the input may now contain negative numbers. Is the product of the two largest values still the answer? 🧠 Checkpoint: Negative numbers Question: What is the maximum pairwise product of [-10, -9, 1, 3] ? Does the linear algorithm still work? Answer: The answer is (-10) \cdot (-9) = 90 , not 1 \cdot 3 = 3 : the product of two negative numbers is positive. With negative numbers allowed, the maximum product is either the product of the two largest values or the product of the two smallest values (the two most negative ones). The algorithm can be adapted by keeping track of four values in the same single pass (the two largest and the two smallest) and returning the larger of the two candidate products. It remains linear in time and constant in memory, but the initial values -1 no longer work as "nothing seen yet" and must be replaced (for example, by the first two elements). Note how a small change in the specification invalidates a key step of the reasoning. Correctness is always relative to a specification.

Step Problem detected Lesson 1. Two int numbers Silent arithmetic overflow. Respect the limits of data types. 2. Using long long r = a * b still overflows with int operands. Promote operands before operating. 3. Realistic input Toy examples hide problems. Test with realistic sizes and predict the result. 4. Brute force Correct, but its cost grows quadratically. Hardware cannot fix a bad growth rate. 5. Sort descending Much faster, but modifies the input. Change the strategy; watch out for side effects. 6. Sort ascending Same growth, less work. Distinguish growth rate from constant factors. 7. Linear scan Optimal in time and memory. Find exactly what you need, nothing more. Stress testing Plausible "optimizations" can be wrong. Compare fast versions against a trusted slow one. The rest of this chapter gives us the tools to make these intuitions precise: how to measure and count the cost of an algorithm, and how to describe its growth with asymptotic notation.
