t: Complexity Analysis: Counting the Cost of an Algorithm

s.x: ⏱ 14 min read Read first: Measuring Efficiency · Sums, Logarithms and Factorials In the previous lesson we saw that measurements depend on the machine, the compiler and the implementation, and that comparing algorithms only by running them has serious limitations. We now develop the alternative: studying the algorithm on paper , by counting how many elementary operations it performs as a function of the size of its input. The result is a function, T(n) , that describes the cost of the algorithm independently of any particular computer. It allows us to compare algorithms before implementing them, to predict their behavior for large inputs and to understand why one is better than another. What you will learn in this lesson The cost model used to analyze algorithms: elementary operations that take one unit of time. How to obtain T(n) by counting how many times each instruction executes, for loops, conditionals and method calls. The summation formulas that appear most often when analyzing loops. Why the cost of an algorithm can depend on the content of the input, and how we handle it with the best , worst and average cases. How to analyze the memory an algorithm needs, S(n) , including the call stack.

To analyze an algorithm mathematically, we use an idealised computer with the following rules: Elementary operations take exactly one unit of time (u.t.) : assigning a value, an arithmetic operation, a comparison, a logical operation, accessing an element of an array, returning from a method... Instructions are executed one after another (no parallelism). Memory is unlimited and accessing any position takes the same time. This model is a deliberate simplification. In a real processor a division is slower than an addition, and accessing data that is in the cache is much faster than accessing main memory. But all these differences are bounded by constants : a division may cost, say, 20 times more than an addition, but never n times more. Since our goal is to understand how the cost grows with n , constant factors do not change the conclusions, as the next lesson will make precise. Not every line of code is elementary A line such as Arrays.sort(v) , list.contains(x) or text.indexOf(word) looks like a single instruction, but it executes a whole algorithm whose cost depends on the size of the data. When analyzing a program, always ask how much a library call really costs. In the exercises of this course, we will make it explicit, for example by writing instruction_O(n) for an operation whose cost grows linearly.

As we saw in the previous lesson, the cost is expressed as a function of the size of the input , n : the number of elements of a vector, of a matrix or of the records of a table, the number of nodes of a graph, etc. Sometimes more than one parameter is needed: the cost of an algorithm on a graph usually depends on both the number of nodes and the number of edges, and the cost of processing an r \times c matrix depends on both dimensions.

s.h: Counting Operations: The Sum of a Vector
s.x: Let us calculate the exact execution time T(n) of an algorithm that sums all the integers of an array. public static int sum ( int [ ] list ) { int value = 0 ; for ( int i = 0 ; i < list . length ; i ++ ) { value += list [ i ] ; } return value ; } 🧠 Checkpoint: Before reading on Question: Counting each elementary instruction as one unit, which of these expressions is the execution time of this method? (a) 2n (b) 3n+4 (c) 3n+3 (d) 2n+3 Answer: (b) 3n+4 . Check it with the table below. The most common mistake is to forget that the loop condition is evaluated one extra time, the one that returns false and ends the loop. Let us count how many times each instruction is executed, with n = list.length : Line Instruction Executions Explanation 2 int value = 0; 1 Runs once, at the beginning. 3 int i = 0; 1 The initialization of the loop runs once. 3 i < list.length n + 1 Checked before each of the n iterations, plus one final time that evaluates to false . 3 i++ n Executed at the end of each iteration. 4 value += list[i]; n The body of the loop runs n times. 6 return value; 1 Runs once, at the end. Adding up the executions: T(n) = 1 + 1 + (n + 1) + n + n + 1 = 3n + 4 For an array of 1,000 elements, this model predicts 3,004 elementary operations. How precise is "exact"? Is value += list[i] one operation, or three (read list[i] , add, assign)? Is i++ one or two? Different authors count differently, and they would obtain T(n) = 5n + 4 or 6n + 4 instead of 3n + 4 . All these answers have something essential in common: they are proportional to n for large values of n . The constants depend on arbitrary counting decisions (and, in reality, on the machine), while the growth does not. This is the key motivation for the asymptotic notation of the next lesson.

When loops are nested, or when the number of iterations of the inner loop depends on the outer one, counting line by line becomes cumbersome. Instead, we express the number of executions of the innermost instruction as a summation and simplify it.

Summation Closed form Typical origin \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 n A simple loop. \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} An inner loop that runs i times (triangular loops). \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} i^2 \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} Three nested loops with dependent limits. \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{k} 2^i 2^{k+1} - 1 Quantities that double at each step. \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{k} r^i \dfrac{r^{k+1} - 1}{r - 1} (for r \ne 1 ) Geometric growth with ratio r .

for ( int i = 0 ; i < n ; i ++ ) for ( int j = i + 1 ; j < n ; j ++ ) count ++ ; // how many times? For each value of i , the inner loop runs n - 1 - i times. Therefore: \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (n - 1 - i) = (n-1) + (n-2) + \cdots + 1 + 0 = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} This is exactly the "half of the pairs" version of the brute-force pairwise product: about n^2/2 executions, which still grows quadratically.

s.h: Example 2: a loop that doubles its counter
s.x: for ( int i = 1 ; i <= n ; i *= 2 ) count ++ ; // how many times? The counter takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, \dots, 2^k , and the loop stops when 2^k > n . The number of iterations is the number of powers of 2 that do not exceed n : \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1 For n = 1{,}000{,}000 that is only 20 iterations. Loops whose counter is multiplied or divided by a constant run a logarithmic number of times, a pattern that we will meet in binary search and in divide and conquer algorithms.

long total = 0 ; for ( int r = 0 ; r < rows ; r ++ ) for ( int c = 0 ; c < cols ; c ++ ) total += matrix [ r ] [ c ] ; The body executes rows \cdot cols times. If we take n as the number of elements of the matrix, the algorithm is linear in n . If the matrix is square and we take n as its order (number of rows), the same algorithm executes n^2 times. Both statements are correct: what changes is the meaning of n , which is why it must always be stated explicitly.

Sequence. The cost of a sequence of instructions is the sum of their costs. Conditional ( if (c) A else B ). The cost is the cost of evaluating the condition plus the cost of the branch that is executed. Since we may not know which branch will run, we consider the most expensive one when we want an upper bound, and this naturally leads to distinguishing cases (see below). Loop. The cost is the sum, over all iterations, of the cost of the condition and the body, plus one final evaluation of the condition. Method call. The cost is the cost of the code of the method, applied to the size of its arguments, plus a constant for the call itself. When the method is recursive, this leads to equations in which T(n) is defined in terms of T applied to smaller sizes ( recurrences ), which you will learn to solve in the divide and conquer chapter.

For the sum of a vector, T(n) depends only on n : the loop always performs the same work, whatever the values in the vector. But for many algorithms, two inputs of the same size can require very different amounts of work. Consider searching for a value: public static boolean contains ( int [ ] list , int value ) { for ( int i = 0 ; i < list . length ; i ++ ) if ( list [ i ] == value ) return true ; // found: stop immediately return false ; } Three searches in the same array of size 8. The size is the same, but the work goes from 1 comparison (the value is first) to 8 (the value is not there). If the value is in the first position, the method returns after one iteration. If it is not in the vector, it must inspect all n elements. To characterise algorithms like this one, we distinguish three cases: 🔴 Worst case 🟢 Best case 🟡 Average case Definition: T_{worst}(n) is the maximum time of the algorithm over all inputs of size n . For contains , it corresponds to the value not being present (or being in the last position): all n elements are inspected. Value: it is a guarantee : the algorithm will never take longer, whatever the input. This is the case that is analyzed most often, and the essential one in critical systems that must respond within a deadline (aircraft, medical devices, industrial control). Definition: T_{best}(n) is the minimum time over all inputs of size n . For contains , it is the value being in the first position: one iteration, whatever the value of n . Value: limited, and sometimes deceptive. Some "best cases" are very unlikely to happen in practice. However, it can be informative: some sorting algorithms, for example, are very fast on data that is already sorted or almost sorted, and that situation does happen in real applications. Definition: T_{average}(n) is the expected time over the inputs of size n . If the possible situations (cases) are numbered 1, 2, \dots, N , and case i happens with probability P_i and takes time T_i(n) , then: T_{average}(n) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} P_i \cdot T_i(n) Value: apparently, it is the most reasonable measure, because it describes what we should expect "normally". But it has two difficulties: it requires knowing (or assuming) the probability distribution of the inputs, which may not reflect reality, and the calculation is usually harder than for the other cases.

Suppose that the value we look for is in the vector, and that it is equally likely to be in any position, so each position has probability 1/n . If it is in position i (counting from 1), contains inspects i elements. The expected number of inspected elements is: \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{n} \cdot i = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{n+1}{2} On average, we inspect about half of the vector: still proportional to n . In the lesson on searching we will repeat this analysis counting every instruction, and also considering the possibility that the value is not present. 🧠 Checkpoint: Which case? Question: For the maximum pairwise product algorithms of the case study (brute force, sorting, linear scan), do the best, worst and average cases differ? Answer: For brute force and for the linear scan, essentially no: both always traverse the same loops completely, whatever the values (only the number of times the if body executes changes, which does not affect the growth). For the version based on sorting, it depends on the sorting algorithm: some sorting algorithms (such as the TimSort used by Java for objects) are much faster when the data is already sorted. Analyzing the cases always requires looking at which inputs make the algorithm work more or less . Amortised cost There is a fourth way of looking at cost, which we mentioned when studying ArrayList : the amortised cost, which is the average cost per operation over a sequence of operations , in the worst case. It does not involve probabilities. An ArrayList occasionally performs an expensive copy when it grows, but over any long sequence of insertions the average cost per insertion is constant.

Time is not the only resource. The space complexity S(n) measures the additional memory that an algorithm needs, as a function of the size of the input, beyond the memory occupied by the input itself. It is analyzed with the same counting approach: how many variables, and of what size, does the algorithm create? The sum of a vector needs two variables ( value and i ), whatever the value of n : its additional space is constant . An algorithm that copies the input into a new array, or that creates an auxiliary array of the same size (as Mergesort does), needs space proportional to n . In-place and out-of-place algorithms An algorithm is in place when it transforms the input using only a constant (or very small) amount of additional memory, such as a few variables. An algorithm is out of place when it needs additional memory that grows with the input, such as auxiliary arrays or copies.

Recursive algorithms consume memory even if they do not create any data structure: each active call occupies a frame on the call stack. The recursive factorial of the first lesson performs n nested calls before reaching the base case, so it needs stack space proportional to n ; the iterative version needs constant space. This is why a deep recursion can end with a StackOverflowError even when the algorithm is correct.

Time and space are often exchanged: we can sometimes save a lot of time by storing results that would otherwise have to be recomputed (the main idea of dynamic programming), or save memory at the cost of recomputing. An engineer must consider both resources and choose the balance that fits the constraints of the problem.

We analyze algorithms in an idealised model in which each elementary operation costs one unit of time. Library calls are not necessarily elementary. T(n) is obtained by counting how many times each instruction executes. For the sum of a vector, T(n) = 3n + 4 . Nested and dependent loops are counted with summations ; loops whose counter is multiplied or divided by a constant run a logarithmic number of times. The exact constants depend on counting conventions, but the growth does not. When the cost depends on the content of the input, we distinguish the best , worst and average cases. The worst case is a guarantee; the average case requires assumptions about probabilities. S(n) measures the additional memory , including the call stack used by recursion.

🧮 Count it. Obtain T(n) , counting each instruction as one unit, for a method that returns the maximum of a non-empty vector of n integers. Does the result depend on the content of the vector? (Hint: the assignment inside the if may or may not execute.) 📐 Use summations. How many times does the innermost instruction run in this fragment? for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < i; j++) for (k = 0; k < j; k++) x++; Give the exact formula and its leading term. 🔢 Logarithmic loops. How many iterations does for (i = n; i >= 1; i /= 3) perform? Check your formula for n = 1 , n = 9 and n = 10 . ⚖️ Cases. For a method that checks whether a vector is sorted in ascending order (returning false as soon as it finds two consecutive elements out of order), describe the best and worst cases and their cost. 💾 Space. Compare the additional space needed by the three versions of the maximum pairwise product (brute force, sorting a copy, linear scan). 💻 Verify experimentally. Add a counter to the sum of a vector that increments once per elementary operation, run it for several values of n and check that the result is 3n + 4 .

t: Complexity of Loops: A Catalog of Patterns

s.x: ⏱ 13 min read Read first: Asymptotic Notation · Sums, Logarithms and Factorials Most iterative algorithms are, at their core, combinations of loops. Once you can determine quickly and reliably how many times a loop runs, you can analyze almost any iterative program. This lesson collects the most common patterns, explains how to derive each result and points out the traps that appear most often in exams and in real code. Throughout the lesson, O(1) in the body of a loop means "some work whose cost does not depend on n ", and instruction_O(f(n)) means an instruction whose cost is O(f(n)) . What you will learn in this lesson The general rules for sequences, loops, nested loops and conditionals. How the step of a loop (adding, multiplying, dividing) determines whether it is linear or logarithmic. How to analyze nested loops whose limits depend on each other, using summations. How to combine patterns, and some less obvious cases: \sqrt{n} loops and harmonic sums. The typical mistakes to avoid.

Sequence. For instructions s_1, s_2, \dots, s_k executed one after another, the cost is O(s_1) + O(s_2) + \cdots + O(s_k) , which is the order of the largest one. Loop. The cost is the sum of the costs of all its iterations . When every iteration costs the same, this is simply number of iterations × cost of the body . Nested loops. Analyze from the inside out : compute the cost of the inner loop (possibly depending on the variable of the outer one), then sum over the iterations of the outer loop. Conditional. The cost of evaluating the condition plus the cost of the branch that is executed. For an upper bound, take the most expensive branch; for a precise analysis, count how many times each branch is executed. Method call. The cost of the method for the size of its arguments. The key quantity is always the number of iterations , and it depends on three things: the initial value , the final condition and the step of the loop variable.

When the loop variable is increased or decreased by a constant amount, the number of iterations is proportional to the distance it has to cover: for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } // n iterations → O(n) for ( i = n ; i > 0 ; i -- ) { O ( 1 ) } // n iterations → O(n) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i += 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // about n/2 iterations → O(n) for ( i = 1 ; i <= 3 * n ; i += 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // about 3n/2 iterations → O(n) for ( i = 1 ; i <= c1 * n ; i += c2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // about c1·n/c2 → O(n) In general, if the variable must travel a distance proportional to n with a constant step, the loop runs about \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{step}} times, which is O(n) . Changing the step from 1 to 2 halves the work, but does not change the complexity : the constant disappears in the O . The distance matters, not only the step for (i = 1; i <= n*n; i += 2) runs about n^2/2 times: it is O(n^2) , not O(n) , because the distance is n^2 . And for (i = n/2; i <= n; i++) runs about n/2 times: still O(n) , because half of n is proportional to n .

When the loop variable is multiplied or divided by a constant at each step, it reaches its limit very quickly: for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i *= 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // log2(n) + 1 iterations → O(log n) for ( i = n ; i >= 1 ; i /= 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // log2(n) + 1 iterations → O(log n) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i *= c ) { O ( 1 ) } // logc(n) + 1 iterations → O(log n) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n * n ; i *= 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // log2(n²) = 2·log2(n) → O(log n) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n * n * n / 2 ; i *= c ) { O ( 1 ) } // logc(n³/2) → O(log n) Why? After k iterations of the first loop, i = 2^k . The loop stops when 2^k \gt n , that is, when k \gt \log_2 n . So it runs \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1 times. The same reasoning with base c gives \log_c n iterations for the third loop. Doubling the counter: the jumps grow so fast that only 7 iterations fit below n = 100. Doubling n adds just one more jump. The last two examples show the power of the logarithm rules from the asymptotic notation lesson: going up to n^2 or n^3/2 instead of n only multiplies the number of iterations by a constant, since \log(n^k) = k \log n and \log(n^3/2) = 3 \log n - \log 2 . All of them are O(\log n) . A classic infinite loop for (i = 0; i < n; i *= 2) never ends : 0 \cdot 2 = 0 . Multiplicative loops must start at a positive value. Similarly, i /= 2 with integers eventually reaches 0, so a condition like i >= 0 would never become false.

When the limits of the inner loop do not depend on the outer variable, the costs simply multiply : for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) for ( j = 1 ; j <= n ; j ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } // n · n = n² → O(n²) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) for ( j = 1 ; j <= n ; j *= 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // n · log n → O(n log n)

When the inner loop depends on the outer variable, we sum. A typical case is the triangular loop: for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) for ( j = i + 1 ; j <= n ; j ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } For each i , the inner loop runs n - i times: \sum_{i=1}^{n} (n - i) = (n-1) + (n-2) + \cdots + 1 + 0 = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \in O(n^2) The triangular loop for n = 6. Each green cell is one execution of the body: row i has n − i of them, and together they fill half of the n × n square. The inner loop is shorter on average (about n/2 iterations instead of n ), but that only affects the constant: the result is still quadratic.

for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) for ( j = n ; j >= 1 ; j -- ) for ( k = 1 ; k <= j ; k ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } The innermost loop runs j times. Summing from the inside out: \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} j = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = n \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \in O(n^3) Note that the direction of the middle loop (decreasing) does not matter: what matters is the set of values j takes. for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) for ( j = i ; j <= n ; j ++ ) for ( k = j ; k <= n ; k ++ ) for ( p = k ; p <= n ; p ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } Here each loop starts from the value of the previous one, so the body runs once for each combination 1 \le i \le j \le k \le p \le n . The exact count is \binom{n+3}{4} = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}{24} , which is O(n^4) . In general, m nested loops whose ranges are proportional to n give O(n^m) , even if the dependencies reduce the constant (here, by a factor of 24). A quick rule and its limits For nested loops whose ranges are all proportional to n (even if they depend on each other in a "triangular" way), the complexity is n raised to the number of nested loops. But be careful: this rule fails when a loop is logarithmic or when its range is not proportional to n , as the next patterns show. When in doubt, write the summation.

Most real loops combine the previous patterns. The approach is always the same: determine the number of iterations of each loop, and multiply them if they are independent. // (a) for ( i = 2 * n ; i >= 0 ; i -= 3 ) // about 2n/3 iterations: O(n) for ( j = 1 ; j <= n * n * n ; j *= 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // log2(n³) = 3·log2(n): O(log n) // Total: O(n log n) // (b) for ( i = n ; i >= 1 ; i /= 2 ) // log2(n) iterations: O(log n) for ( j = 1 ; j <= n / 3 ; j ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } // n/3 iterations: O(n) // Total: O(n log n) // (c) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i *= 3 ) // log3(n) iterations: O(log n) for ( j = 1 ; j <= n * n * n ; j *= 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // 3·log2(n) iterations: O(log n) // Total: O(log² n) // (d) for ( i = n / 2 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) // n/2 iterations: O(n) for ( j = 1 ; j <= n / 3 ; j += 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // n/6 iterations: O(n) // Total: O(n²) Example (c) is worth remembering: two nested logarithmic loops give O(\log^2 n) , that is, (\log n)^2 , which is not the same as O(\log n) but is still far below O(n) . Example (d) shows that loops covering only a fraction of the range ( n/2 to n , or up to n/3 ) are still linear.

When the body is not constant, multiply by its cost: for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) instruction_O ( n ) ; // n · O(n) = O(n²) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i *= 2 ) instruction_O ( n ) ; // log n · O(n) = O(n log n)

When a loop contains a conditional with branches of different cost, a precise analysis counts how many times each branch executes: for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) if ( i % 10 == 0 ) instruction_O ( n ) ; // runs n/10 times else instruction_O ( 1 ) ; // runs 9n/10 times The expensive branch runs n/10 times, contributing \frac{n}{10} \cdot O(n) = O(n^2) ; the cheap one contributes O(n) . The total is O(n^2) . If, instead, the expensive branch ran only a constant number of times (for example, only when i == 1 ), it would contribute just O(n) and the total would be O(n) . Taking the most expensive branch for every iteration always gives a valid upper bound, but it may not be the tightest one.

for ( i = 1 ; i * i <= n ; i ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } The loop stops when i^2 \gt n , that is, when i \gt \sqrt{n} , so it runs \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor times: O(\sqrt{n}) . This is the pattern of the classic primality test, which only needs to try divisors up to \sqrt{n} .

for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) for ( j = 1 ; j <= n ; j += i ) { O ( 1 ) } The inner loop advances in steps of i , so it runs about n/i times. The total is: \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{n}{i} = n \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i} = n \cdot H_n \approx n \ln n \in O(n \log n) where H_n is the harmonic number , which grows like \ln n . This pattern (an inner loop that becomes shorter and shorter, in proportion 1/i ) appears, for example, in the sieve of Eratosthenes.

while loops are analyzed exactly like for loops: identify the variable that controls the loop, its initial value, how it changes in each iteration, and the condition that stops it. int i = n ; while ( i > 1 ) { O ( 1 ) ; i = i / 2 ; } The variable is halved at each iteration, so this is Pattern 2: O(\log n) . Sometimes the variable that controls the loop is not obvious (it may be the size of a data structure, or the distance between two indices, as in binary search); finding it is the first step of the analysis.

Counting loops instead of iterations. Two nested loops are not always O(n^2) : if one of them is logarithmic, the result is O(n \log n) ; if the inner one runs a constant number of times, it is O(n) . Forgetting the range. A loop up to n^2 with an additive step is quadratic, not linear. Confusing \log(n^k) with \log^k n . A multiplicative loop up to n^3 is O(\log n) ; two nested logarithmic loops are O(\log^2 n) . Ignoring the cost of the body. Library calls ( contains , indexOf , sort , string concatenation in a loop...) may hide linear or worse costs inside an apparently simple loop. Adding instead of multiplying (or vice versa). Sequential loops add (and the largest one dominates); nested loops multiply . 🧠 Checkpoint: Analyze these fragments Question: Determine the complexity of each fragment. // (1) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) for ( j = 1 ; j <= 100 ; j ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } // (2) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } for ( j = 1 ; j <= n ; j ++ ) for ( k = 1 ; k <= n ; k *= 2 ) { O ( 1 ) } // (3) for ( i = 1 ; i <= n ; i *= 2 ) for ( j = 1 ; j <= i ; j ++ ) { O ( 1 ) } Answer: O(n) . The inner loop runs 100 times, a constant, whatever the value of n . O(n \log n) . The two parts are sequential: O(n) + O(n \log n) = O(n \log n) . O(n) , a surprising one. The inner loop runs i times, and i takes the values 1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^k with 2^k \le n . The total is 1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 2^k = 2^{k+1} - 1 \lt 2n . Multiplying " \log n iterations × up to n per iteration" would give O(n \log n) , a valid but not tight bound. This is why dependent loops must be summed .

The patterns of this lesson are easy to verify experimentally with the techniques of the lesson on measuring efficiency: implement a loop, measure its time for increasing sizes, and check the ratio between consecutive times. A quadratic loop should multiply its time by about 4 when n doubles, a cubic one by about 8, and a loop of O(n \log n) by a little more than 2. In the lab sessions you will do exactly this, both with given loops and with loops you design yourself to have a given complexity.

The number of iterations of a loop depends on its initial value , final condition and step . Additive steps over a range proportional to n give O(n) ; multiplicative steps give O(\log n) , even if the range is n^2 or n^3 . Independent nested loops multiply; dependent ones are analyzed with summations . Sequential code adds, and the largest term dominates. Watch out for O(\sqrt{n}) loops, harmonic sums ( O(n \log n) ) and geometric sums (which can turn an apparent O(n \log n) into O(n) ).

🔍 Classify. Give the complexity of for (i = n; i > 1; i = i / 3) for (j = 0; j < i * i; j++) { O(1) } . Is it O(n^2 \log n) ? (Hint: sum the iterations of the inner loop, as in the last checkpoint.) 📏 Count exactly. How many times does the body of for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) for (j = 1; j <= i * i; j++) { O(1) } run? Give the exact formula and its order. 🧩 Find the trap. String s = ""; for (i = 0; i < n; i++) s += "x"; Strings in Java are immutable: each concatenation creates a new string, copying the previous one. What is the complexity of the loop? How does StringBuilder change it? 🛠️ Design. Write a loop whose complexity is O(\sqrt{n} \log n) , and another one whose complexity is O(n \sqrt{n}) . 💻 Verify. Implement two of the patterns of this lesson, measure them with the doubling test (without optimization) and check that the ratios match the theoretical complexity.

t: Data Structures: The Other Half of Every Program

s.x: ⏱ 18 min read Read first: Algorithmic Thinking In the previous lessons we saw that the efficiency of a solution depends on the strategy we choose. It also depends, just as much, on how the data is organized in memory . The maximum pairwise product already gave us a hint: the same algorithm used several times more memory with a List<Integer> than with an int[] . Algorithms require an adequate representation of the data to achieve efficient results. Such representations, together with the operations allowed on them, are called data structures . Most current programming languages offer a very similar set of them, so what you learn here with Java transfers almost directly to other languages. What you will learn in this lesson Why data structures remain essential even though computers keep getting faster. The difference between an abstract data type (what operations are offered) and a data structure (how they are implemented). The primitive types of Java and their limits, and the strengths and weaknesses of arrays. The main interfaces and implementations of the Java Collections Framework , the cost of their operations and how they behave in practice. How these structures map to C# (.NET) and Python. The basic vocabulary of graphs and trees , which will appear throughout the course.

Niklaus Wirth's famous formula, Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs , expresses an idea that you will see in every chapter of this course: the two cannot be designed separately. An algorithm that needs to check many times whether an element belongs to a collection will be slow on a list and fast on a hash set. A sorting algorithm that is excellent on arrays may be poor on linked lists. Choosing the data structure is part of designing the algorithm.

s.h: Are data structures really that important?
s.x: Processor speed and memory size keep increasing. A natural question is whether any challenging problem we face today will simply be solved by tomorrow's hardware, making careful data organization unnecessary. History says no. As computers become more powerful, we have always used the additional power to tackle more complex problems : Bigger problem sizes: more users, more transactions, higher resolutions, larger genomes, larger language models. New problems that were previously considered computationally infeasible. As we saw in the case study, a better machine cannot compensate for a bad growth rate. The same applies to data structures: a structure whose operations become slower as the collection grows will eventually be the bottleneck, whatever the hardware.

s.h: Abstract data types and data structures
s.x: It is useful to distinguish two levels: An abstract data type (ADT) describes a collection of values and the operations allowed on them, without saying how they are implemented. For example, a stack is defined by push , pop and peek , with the rule that the last element pushed is the first one popped (LIFO). A data structure is a concrete implementation of an ADT in memory: an array, a chain of linked nodes, a tree, a hash table... The same ADT can be implemented by several data structures with very different costs. In Java this distinction appears naturally as interfaces ( List , Set , Map ...) and classes that implement them ( ArrayList , LinkedList , HashSet , TreeSet ...). This is the principle of abstraction from the first lesson: we program against the interface and choose the implementation that best fits the operations we will perform most often.

The most basic data structures are the primitive types offered by the language. In Java, their sizes and ranges are fixed by the language specification, independently of the hardware: Type Category Size Range boolean Logical not specified (usually 1 byte) true , false char Character 2 bytes Unicode characters (UTF-16 code units) byte Integer 1 byte -128 to 127 short Integer 2 bytes -32{,}768 to 32{,}767 int Integer 4 bytes -2^{31} to 2^{31}-1 (about \pm 2.1 \times 10^{9} ) long Integer 8 bytes -2^{63} to 2^{63}-1 (about \pm 9.2 \times 10^{18} ) float Real 4 bytes up to about \pm 3.4 \times 10^{38} , about 7 significant digits double Real 8 bytes up to about \pm 1.8 \times 10^{308} , about 15-16 significant digits Two practical consequences, both relevant for algorithms: Integer overflow is silent , as we saw in the case study: if a result does not fit, it wraps around without warning. Real numbers are approximate. float and double store binary approximations, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false in Java. Never compare real numbers with == ; compare their difference with a small tolerance, and never use them for money.

The array is the most fundamental data structure: a fixed number of elements of the same type stored in consecutive memory positions . It exists in virtually every programming language. Because elements are contiguous and all have the same size, the address of element i can be computed directly as start address + i × element size . That is why accessing any position takes the same time regardless of the size of the array, a property called random access (or constant-time access). An array and a linked list with the same elements. The array computes the address of any element directly; the list must follow the references one by one, but inserting a node only requires changing two references. Arrays also have important limitations: Fixed size. You cannot resize an array once created; growing it means creating a larger one and copying everything. Homogeneous elements. All elements must have the same type. Positional access only. Elements are accessed by their index; finding an element by its value requires inspecting the array (unless it is sorted, as you will see with binary search). Costly insertions and deletions. Inserting or removing an element in the middle requires shifting all the elements after it. No higher-level operations. Arrays do not directly provide sets (without duplicates), stacks, queues, priority queues or dictionaries. These limitations are exactly what the collection libraries of modern languages solve.

Java offers a powerful library for working with collections, the Java Collections Framework (in the java.util package). It improves productivity and quality, because the structures are well tested and optimized, and it is organized around a set of interfaces and their implementations .

Interface Description Iterable Allows iterating over the elements in a forward direction (and using the for-each loop). Collection Extends Iterable to work with groups of objects (add, remove, contains, size...). List Extends Collection to handle sequences : ordered elements, accessible by position, duplicates allowed. Queue Extends Collection for collections whose elements are retrieved from the head, usually in FIFO order (first in, first out). Deque Extends Queue to handle double-ended queues : insertion and removal at both ends, so it can work as FIFO or LIFO. Set Extends Collection to handle sets : no duplicate elements. SortedSet Extends Set to keep the elements sorted in ascending order. Map Not a Collection : stores key-value pairs with unique keys (dictionaries). SortedMap keeps the keys sorted.

Class Implements Internal structure Main features ArrayList List Dynamic (resizable) array Fast access by position; slow insertions in the middle. The default choice for lists. LinkedList List , Deque Doubly linked list Fast insertion and removal at the ends; slow access by position. Vector List Dynamic array Like ArrayList but synchronised (thread-safe). Legacy class. Stack List Dynamic array (extends Vector ) LIFO operations push , pop , peek . Legacy class. PriorityQueue Queue Binary heap Always retrieves the smallest element first (or according to a Comparator ). ArrayDeque Deque Circular resizable array Efficient FIFO queue and LIFO stack. Preferred over Stack and usually over LinkedList . HashSet Set Hash table Very fast add, remove and contains; no guaranteed order . LinkedHashSet Set Hash table + linked list Like HashSet , but iterates in insertion order . TreeSet SortedSet Balanced binary search tree (red-black tree) Keeps elements sorted ; operations slower than hashing but still fast. HashMap / LinkedHashMap / TreeMap Map Same ideas as the corresponding sets Dictionaries with unordered, insertion-ordered or sorted keys.

The following table summarizes how the cost of the most common operations grows with the number of elements n . We describe it informally here; in the following lessons you will learn the precise notation ( O(1) , O(\log n) , O(n) ) used to express these costs. Structure Access by position Search by value Insert / remove at the end Insert / remove at the beginning or middle Array / ArrayList constant linear constant (amortised)¹ linear (shifting) LinkedList linear linear constant constant at the ends; linear to reach the middle ArrayDeque not available linear constant (amortised) constant at the beginning PriorityQueue not available linear insert: logarithmic; remove the minimum: logarithmic not available HashSet / HashMap not available constant on average² constant on average constant on average TreeSet / TreeMap not available logarithmic logarithmic logarithmic ¹ When the internal array of an ArrayList is full, it is replaced by a larger one (about 1.5 times larger) and all elements are copied. That copy is expensive, but it happens so rarely that, on average over a long sequence of insertions , each insertion costs a constant amount of work. This is called amortised cost. ² Hash tables are constant on average if the hash function distributes the elements well. In unfavorable cases, many elements may collide in the same position and operations become slower. Choosing a collection Ask yourself which operations your algorithm will perform most often : Mostly access by position and appends? ArrayList . Queue (FIFO) or stack (LIFO)? ArrayDeque . Always need the smallest (or largest) element? PriorityQueue . Membership tests ("have I seen this before?")? HashSet . Need the elements sorted, or ranges like "all elements between B and E"? TreeSet / TreeMap .

s.h: Collections in Action: What Is the Output?
s.x: The best way to understand the behavior of each collection is to predict the output of small programs. Try to answer each question before opening the solution. All these examples are in the course repository. ArrayList LinkedList Stack PriorityQueue ArrayDeque Sets var collection = new ArrayList < String > ( ) ; collection . add ( "A" ) ; collection . add ( "B" ) ; collection . add ( "C" ) ; collection . add ( "D" ) ; collection . add ( 1 , "A2" ) ; // insert at position 1 System . out . println ( collection . size ( ) + " " + collection ) ; collection . remove ( "A2" ) ; // remove by value collection . remove ( 3 ) ; // remove by position System . out . println ( collection . size ( ) + " " + collection ) ; Show output 5 [A, A2, B, C, D] 3 [A, B, C] add(1, "A2") shifts B, C and D one position to the right. After removing "A2" the list is [A, B, C, D] , and remove(3) removes the element at index 3, which is D. Note that remove is overloaded: with an Object it removes by value, with an int it removes by position. With a List<Integer> this overloading is a classic source of bugs! A Vector produces exactly the same output: the difference is not in the behavior but in synchronisation. var collection = new LinkedList < String > ( ) ; collection . add ( "B" ) ; collection . add ( "C" ) ; collection . add ( "D" ) ; collection . addLast ( "E" ) ; collection . addFirst ( "A" ) ; collection . add ( 1 , "A2" ) ; System . out . println ( collection . size ( ) + " " + collection ) ; collection . remove ( "A2" ) ; collection . remove ( 3 ) ; collection . removeFirst ( ) ; collection . removeLast ( ) ; System . out . println ( collection . size ( ) + " " + collection ) ; Show output 6 [A, A2, B, C, D, E] 2 [B, C] After the additions the list is [A, A2, B, C, D, E] . Removing "A2" gives [A, B, C, D, E] ; remove(3) removes D; removeFirst() removes A and removeLast() removes E. Operations at the ends of a linked list are cheap, but remove(3) must walk through the nodes to reach position 3. var collection = new Stack < String > ( ) ; collection . add ( "A" ) ; collection . add ( "B" ) ; collection . add ( "C" ) ; collection . add ( "D" ) ; collection . add ( 1 , "A2" ) ; collection . pop ( ) ; collection . pop ( ) ; System . out . println ( collection . size ( ) + " " + collection ) ; collection . remove ( "A2" ) ; collection . remove ( 3 ) ; System . out . println ( collection . size ( ) + " " + collection ) ; Show output 3 [A, A2, B] Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Array index out of range: 3 The two pop() calls remove the last elements added at the top: D and then C. After removing "A2" , the stack contains only [A, B] , so remove(3) fails because position 3 does not exist. This example also shows a design flaw of Stack : because it extends Vector , it allows operations such as add(1, ...) or remove(3) that break the LIFO discipline. That is one reason why ArrayDeque is recommended for stacks. var queue = new PriorityQueue < String > ( ) ; queue . add ( "B" ) ; queue . add ( "A" ) ; queue . add ( "C" ) ; queue . add ( "D" ) ; queue . add ( "A" ) ; queue . remove ( "A" ) ; System . out . println ( queue . size ( ) ) ; while ( ! queue . isEmpty ( ) ) { System . out . print ( queue . poll ( ) ) ; } Show output 4 ABCD remove("A") removes only one of the two A's. Then poll() always extracts the smallest remaining element, so the elements come out in alphabetical order. Be careful: if you print the queue directly ( System.out.println(queue) ), the order you see is the internal order of the heap, which is not necessarily sorted. var queue = new ArrayDeque < String > ( ) ; // used as a FIFO queue queue . add ( "B" ) ; queue . add ( "A" ) ; queue . add ( "C" ) ; queue . add ( "D" ) ; queue . add ( "A" ) ; while ( ! queue . isEmpty ( ) ) System . out . print ( queue . poll ( ) ) ; System . out . println ( ) ; var stack = new ArrayDeque < String > ( ) ; // used as a LIFO stack stack . push ( "B" ) ; stack . push ( "A" ) ; stack . push ( "C" ) ; stack . push ( "D" ) ; stack . push ( "A" ) ; stack . add ( "Z" ) ; // add at the TAIL stack . push ( "J" ) ; // push at the HEAD while ( ! stack . isEmpty ( ) ) System . out . print ( stack . pop ( ) ) ; Show output BACDA JADCABZ As a queue, elements come out in the same order they went in (FIFO). As a stack, push and pop work on the head, so elements come out in reverse order (LIFO). The Z , added at the tail with add , is the last one to come out. var hash = new HashSet < String > ( ) ; hash . add ( "A" ) ; hash . add ( "B" ) ; hash . add ( "C" ) ; hash . add ( "D" ) ; System . out . println ( hash . add ( "B" ) ) ; // a duplicate hash . remove ( "A" ) ; hash . remove ( "C" ) ; System . out . println ( hash ) ; var linked = new LinkedHashSet < String > ( ) ; linked . add ( "B" ) ; linked . add ( "A" ) ; linked . add ( "C" ) ; linked . add ( "D" ) ; linked . remove ( "A" ) ; linked . remove ( "D" ) ; System . out . println ( linked ) ; var tree = new TreeSet < String > ( ) ; tree . add ( "D" ) ; tree . add ( "A" ) ; tree . add ( "B" ) ; tree . add ( "C" ) ; tree . add ( "E" ) ; tree . remove ( "A" ) ; System . out . println ( tree + " " + tree . subSet ( "B" , "E" ) ) ; Show output false [B, D] [B, C] [B, C, D, E] [B, C, D] add returns false when the element was already present: sets never store duplicates. A HashSet gives no ordering guarantees . Here it happens to print [B, D] because of how one-letter strings are hashed, but you must never rely on that order. A LinkedHashSet remembers the insertion order (B, A, C, D), so after the removals it prints [B, C] . A TreeSet keeps the elements sorted , regardless of the insertion order, and supports range operations: subSet("B", "E") includes B and excludes E. A map (or dictionary) associates keys with values . Keys are unique: putting a value with an existing key replaces the old value. The two most common implementations are HashMap and LinkedHashMap , together with TreeMap when the keys must be sorted. Map < String , Integer > stock = new HashMap < > ( ) ; // try LinkedHashMap and TreeMap too stock . put ( "pear" , 3 ) ; stock . put ( "apple" , 7 ) ; stock . put ( "kiwi" , 1 ) ; stock . put ( "apple" , 9 ) ; // replaces 7 stock . merge ( "kiwi" , 1 , Integer :: sum ) ; // kiwi = 1 + 1 System . out . println ( stock + " " + stock . get ( "apple" ) + " " + stock . get ( "fig" ) ) ; Running it with the three implementations gives: HashMap: {apple=9, pear=3, kiwi=2} 9 null LinkedHashMap: {pear=3, apple=9, kiwi=2} 9 null TreeMap: {apple=9, kiwi=2, pear=3} 9 null The contents are the same; only the iteration order changes: unspecified for HashMap , insertion order for LinkedHashMap , and alphabetical order of the keys for TreeMap . Note also that get returns null for a missing key. Maps are one of the most useful tools for designing efficient algorithms. For example, counting how many times each word appears in a text takes a single pass with a HashMap , while doing it with lists would require searching the list for every word.

The same abstract data types exist in most languages, often with different names: Java C# (.NET) Python ArrayList<E> List<T> list LinkedList<E> LinkedList<T> (no direct equivalent; collections.deque for the ends) ArrayDeque<E> as a stack / queue Stack<T> / Queue<T> collections.deque PriorityQueue<E> PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> heapq module HashSet<E> HashSet<T> set TreeSet<E> SortedSet<T> (not in the standard library) HashMap<K, V> Dictionary<TKey, TValue> dict (keeps insertion order) TreeMap<K, V> SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue> (not in the standard library) The names change, but the trade-offs remain the same: dynamic arrays for positional access, hash tables for fast membership, balanced trees for sorted data and heaps for priorities.

Many problems in this course are naturally modelled as graphs : road networks, social networks, dependencies between tasks, states of a game... A graph is a set of nodes (or vertices) connected by a set of edges (or arcs). Formally, a graph is a pair G = \langle N, A \rangle , where N is a set of nodes and A is a set of edges, each connecting two nodes. In a directed graph , edges have a direction: an edge from u to v does not imply an edge from v to u (for example, one-way streets, or "follows" in a social network). In an undirected graph , edges have no direction (for example, two-way roads, or friendship). In a weighted graph , each edge has an associated value: a distance, a cost, a time... A sequence of consecutive edges forms a path . A path that starts and ends at the same node is a cycle . A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of nodes.

The two classical representations have different costs, which is another example of how the data structure affects the algorithm: Adjacency matrix: an |N| \times |N| matrix where cell (u, v) indicates whether there is an edge (or its weight). Checking whether two nodes are connected is immediate, but the memory grows with |N|^2 , even if the graph has few edges. Adjacency lists: for each node, a list of its neighbours. The memory grows with |N| + |A| , which is much better for sparse graphs (few edges), and traversing the neighbours of a node is efficient. Checking whether a specific edge exists, however, requires searching a list. The same undirected graph stored as an adjacency matrix (every pair of nodes has a cell) and as adjacency lists (each node keeps only its neighbors).

Some of the classic graph algorithms that you may meet in this course and in your degree are: Shortest paths: breadth-first search (for unweighted graphs), Dijkstra's algorithm (non-negative weights), the Bellman-Ford algorithm (which allows negative weights) and the Floyd-Warshall algorithm (shortest paths between all pairs of nodes). Minimum spanning trees (connecting all nodes with the minimum total weight): Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms.

A tree consists of a set of nodes and a set of edges connecting pairs of nodes that form a hierarchical structure. It has the following features: It has a distinguished node called the root . Every node c except the root is connected by an edge to exactly one node p : p is the parent of c , and c is one of the children of p . There is exactly one path from the root to each node. The number of edges traversed along a path is its length . Some additional vocabulary: nodes without children are leaves ; the depth of a node is the length of the path from the root to it; and the height of the tree is the maximum depth of its nodes. A tree is a special case of a graph: a connected graph without cycles. Tree vocabulary. Node 1 is the root, nodes 4, 6 and 7 are leaves, and the height of the tree is 3, the depth of its deepest node.

Binary trees , where each node has at most two children: Perfectly balanced trees , where, for every node, the number of nodes in its left and right subtrees differ by at most one. Binary search trees , where every node is greater than all the nodes of its left subtree and smaller than all the nodes of its right subtree, which allows searching by following a single path from the root. Variants include balanced search trees (such as AVL and red-black trees, used by TreeSet and TreeMap ), optimal trees (built according to the frequency with which each key is searched) and splay trees (which move recently accessed elements towards the root). Expression trees , which represent arithmetic expressions: operators in internal nodes, operands in the leaves. Binary heaps , where every node is smaller than (or equal to) its children, so the minimum is always at the root. They are the structure behind PriorityQueue . Multiway trees , where nodes can have many children, such as B-trees , widely used in databases and file systems because they minimize disk accesses. The same seven keys in two binary search trees. Inserted in a good order they form a balanced tree of height 2; inserted in sorted order they form a chain of height 6, no better than a list. Why balance matters In a search tree, the cost of an operation depends on the height of the tree. A balanced tree with n nodes has a height of about \log_2 n : about 20 levels for a million elements. A degenerate tree (for example, one built by inserting already sorted keys into a plain binary search tree) can have height n , and then it is no better than a linked list. Keeping the tree balanced is what makes TreeSet and TreeMap efficient.

Data structures and algorithms are designed together: the same algorithm can be fast or slow depending on how the data is organized. An abstract data type defines operations; a data structure implements them. In Java: interfaces and classes. Primitive types have fixed limits: integers overflow silently and real numbers are approximate. Arrays offer constant-time access by position but have a fixed size and expensive insertions in the middle. The Java Collections Framework provides lists, queues, deques, sets and maps with different cost profiles. Choose according to the operations you perform most often. Graphs and trees model relationships and hierarchies, and their representation affects the cost of the algorithms that use them.

💻 Run the examples. All the "What is the output?" programs are in the course repository , in src/topics/foundation/structures . Modify them and predict the new output before running them. 👀 Visualize the structures. The Data Structure Visualizations by David Galles let you watch step by step how stacks and queues behave when implemented with arrays or linked lists , as well as heaps, search trees and hash tables. ⏱️ Measure the difference. Explain the results using the cost table above. 🔍 List or set? Write a program that checks, for each number of a list of n random integers, whether it has appeared before. Implement it with a List (using contains ) and with a HashSet , and compare the times for n = 10{,}000 , 20{,}000 and 40{,}000 . How does the time grow in each case? 📺 Learn more.
